blocks.text: RETREAT. Leaders gather for the 49th ASEAN Summit retreat session at the Coconut Palace in Pasay City on November 15, 2026.
ASEAN Philippines 2026
‘Konti na lang pag-uusapan nila sa Singapore,’ says Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, as Singapore becomes ASEAN chair in 2027

MANILA, Philippines – The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and China will not meet their deadline to conclude negotiations for the long-delayed Code of Conduct (COC) in the South China Sea under the chairmanship of the Philippines in 2026.
On Sunday, November 15, Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro said ASEAN and China have reached provisional agreement on over 80% of the draft text.

“The negotiations now enter their final phase and we commend the dedication and constructive engagement of all delegations,” Lazaro said in a briefing on the opening day of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

“The parties agree to continue to work constructively with a view to concluding the negotiations on an effective and substantive Code of Conduct at the earliest possible time,” she said, reading from the detailed briefing statement.
The proposed COC is aimed at setting rules for ASEAN and China to follow to reduce tensions in the South China Sea.
China and several ASEAN member states, including the Philippines, have overlapping claims in the resource-rich waterway.
The pending milestone issues are whether the COC will be legally binding, its geographic scope, and how terms would be defined in the code.
A provisional agreement was reached regarding the relationship between the non-binding 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) and the proposed COC.
Lazaro said the parties affirmed that the existing DOC will provide the foundation for the proposed COC.
The COC will also set out “more effective and substantive provisions” to guide conduct in the South China Sea.

“The parties now agree that the Code of Conduct, in addition to guiding conduct, will serve as a platform for practical maritime cooperation in the South China Sea,” Lazaro also said, adding that maritime cooperation would be on a “voluntary basis” and would respect “the sovereignty, sovereign rights, and jurisdiction of coastal states.”
In addition, they agreed that “the COC is intended to serve as a mechanism for the constructive management of differences at sea, and not to settle disputes,” according to Lazaro.
In 2023, ASEAN foreign ministers set 2026 as the deadline for the conclusion of talks on the proposed COC.

With negotiations on crucial issues still not completed, Lazaro sought to explain some of the “sensitivities,” such as potential ratification on the part of certain ASEAN member states in order to make the proposed document legally binding.
“I think there was not enough time. If we were given probably another five to six months, palagay ko (I think) we can finish that,” Lazaro said of the talks.
As ASEAN chair in 2026, the Philippines initiated nine rounds of negotiations and two senior officials’ meetings for the COC.
Lazaro said the proposed text was only at 50% before the country’s shepherding.
“Konti na lang pag-uusapan nila sa Singapore (They have few details left to talk about in Singapore),” she also said, adding that she trusts Singapore will be able to finish the discussions.
Singapore will assume the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027. – Rappler.com

articles.title: PNP stands firm vs alleged attempts to disrupt ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday vowed to stand firm against alleged repeated attempts by protesters to disrupt the country's hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 9:54am
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday vowed to stand firm against alleged repeated attempts by protesters to disrupt the country's hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.
In a statement, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said sufficient police personnel would remain deployed at summit venues.
“Hindi nagkulang ang inyong PNP sa pakiusap at paalala sa ating mga kababayan na ilagay sa tamang lugar at panahon ang pagsasagawa ng protesta,” Nartatez said.
(Your PNP has not failed to ask and remind our countrymen to hold the protest at the right place and time.)
“Hindi po ugali ng mga Pilipino ang mambastos at ilagay sa alanganin ang seguridad ng ating mga bisita,” he said.
(It is not the habit of Filipinos to be rude and jeopardize the security of our guests.)

Nartatez said police commanders had repeatedly appealed to protesters to conduct their activities peacefully and away from summit venues. However, he said police personnel had to enforce the law after protesters supposedly disregarded their appeals and affected public order.
According to the PNP, some protesters allegedly tried to break the police line to hold their activities at the ASEAN Summit venues.

Nartatez said the PNP would continue to observe maximum tolerance and maintain a defensive posture but would not allow any action that could compromise the safety of ASEAN leaders, delegates, visitors, and other guests.
“While we maintain a defensive posture and continue to observe maximum tolerance, we will not allow any action that will compromise the safety of any of our guests,” he added.

He also directed the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) and other police units to sustain security measures for the remaining summit activities and remain professional in handling succeeding demonstrations.
Meanwhile, Nartatez defended police personnel deployed to manage the protest actions amid allegations against some of them.
“Let us recognize that our personnel on the ground were performing their duties under challenging circumstances, repeatedly appealing to protesters to cooperate and avoid confrontation,” he said.
“We will stand by our men and women who perform their duties professionally and lawfully, but we assure the public that any deviation from our standards is addressed accordingly,” he added.
On Sunday, Nartatez visited a hospital where two PNP personnel deployed for the ASEAN Summit were confined following separate incidents.
One of the officers was reportedly in a coma, while the other was a motorcycle rider who figured in an accident, according to the PNP. —AOL, GMA News

blocks.text: Australian politician Helen Haines, who lost both of her legs after police say she was deliberately run down with a car, has been discharged from hospital.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He is yet to enter pleas.
Haines, 65, has been discharged, the Alfred Hospital said on Monday, after four weeks and several surgeries which resulted in the amputation of her legs.

Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.
Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.
Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.

MANILA, Philippines — After dropping all 16 bank officials from its witness list, Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team is seeking to summon an anti-money laundering lawyer and three government officials to testify on financial regulations and records involving Cale88 Foods Corp. in her impeachment trial.
In a manifestation dated November 13, the defense asked the Senate impeachment court to issue subpoenas for four witnesses it intends to present during the November 19 and 20 hearings.

The witnesses are being sought in connection with Article II of the articles of impeachment, which covers allegations involving Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) and alleged ill-gotten wealth.
The first proposed witness is Rainer Dela Fuente, a lawyer from AML Consulting PH, whom the defense wants to testify on fundamental legal concepts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act.

The defense also sought subpoenas for three officials from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI), Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and Center for International Expositions and Missions (CITEM).
The officials are being asked to testify and produce certified true copies of government records involving Cale88 Foods Corporation.
They are:

items: Ceferino Rodolfo, DTI undersecretary and Board of Investments managing head, who is being asked to testify on Cale88's BOI registration and submit its registration documents, certificate of registration and related correspondence.

Pilar Marilyn Pagayunan, director IV of the FDA's Center for Food Regulation and Research, who is being asked to testify on the company's registration of its sweetened banana chips product and produce its registration filings and Certificate of Product Registration.

Rowena Mendoza, department manager III at CITEM, or another authorized CITEM representative, who is being asked to testify on communications and invitations sent to Cale88 concerning food expositions. The defense also seeks correspondence between the company and DTI or CITEM.

blocks.text: The request follows the defense's withdrawal of all 16 bank officials it had previously listed as witnesses in the impeachment trial.
On November 12, the defense dropped 15 bank representatives from its witness list, initially retaining only Bank of the Philippine Islands senior vice president Paul Roderick Ysmael.
The following day, the defense also withdrew Ysmael, leaving none of the 16 bank officials to testify.

articles.title: Megaspeed, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia boss, says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’
articles.summary:
Company insists Alice Huang, accused of being a Chinese spy, left business in late 2025

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Huang, left the business in late 2025.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.
Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees.
US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International.
US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported.

Megaspeed in the past three years has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. A US senator asked the commerce department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.
“Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” it’s statement read.

The global facades of Megaspeed International form a puzzling corporate picture, and involve a lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur and a near-empty office in Singapore.

The company on Sunday said: “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate.”
Short seller Culper Research in May this year quoted a Megaspeed employee as saying Alice Huang was “still our boss”, in a report accusing Nvidia of having a “China problem”.
On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company’s “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.

The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February. Police believed she had given them “inaccurate” information, to downplay her role at the company, but released her due to insufficient evidence.
She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Taiwan has also barred her from re-entry, its authorities have said.
Singapore’s initial investigation related to Megaspeed’s potential “false declarations” over the purchase of computer servers.
after newsletter promotion
On Friday, Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.
Megaspeed has previously said there was no evidence of illegal chip transfers.

Its registered Sydney office is home to numerous business and had no Megaspeed signage, mailbox or physical presence when the Guardian visited last week. No one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.

Reuters visited a news agency and lottery retailer, in Seymour, Victoria, an hour’s drive north of Melbourne, where a woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.
Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.

The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said last week that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, the president, Donald Trump, said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. The Guardian was seeking comment from Huang.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3bn.

articles.title: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’
articles.summary: ‘You can do it faster, but can you do it?’ Maria Ressa says in an interview with Rappler, cautioning young learners against relying on AI to do their work

blocks.text: TRUST. Rappler CEO Maria Ressa delivers a keynote speech about trust in the age of AI at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on November 15, 2026.
Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler
‘You can do it faster, but can you do it?’ Maria Ressa says in an interview with Rappler, cautioning young learners against relying on AI to do their work

items: Maria Ressa emphasizes the need for balance, acknowledging that while AI can enhance efficiency, it should not replace essential skills and independent thinking.
She highlights the dangers of chatbots, which can create emotional dependence and blur the lines between fact and fiction.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler chief executive officer and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa warned that growing overreliance on artificial intelligence could weaken critical thinking and harm newsrooms, one of the pillars of democratic societies.

In an interview with Rappler, Ressa discussed how chatbots can “hack” one’s biology, as they’re designed to keep users engaged, even when it may ultimately dull their ability to think and work independently.

“If you use that chatbot to do your assignment, you could get a good grade, but you won’t learn to think,” she said on the sidelines of the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit on Sunday, November 15.

“It’s anthropomorphic, meaning it pretends to be real, like a human being,” Ressa added. “It’s also sycophantic by design, meaning you actually have to tell it to counter you, or else it tells you what it sees you want to hear.”

That is a damaging combination that Ressa points out has already led to real-life harm, citing the case of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old who took his own life after developing emotional dependence on a Character.AI chatbot. His mother subsequently sued the company, alleging that the chatbot contributed to her son’s death.

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’

blocks.text: AI can also damage newsrooms, with Ressa saying that the proliferation of chatbots and AI content is “part of the reason that you can’t tell the difference between fact and fiction,” contributing to the degradation of democracy.
“The world is a world of nuance. It is a world of learning. Don’t outsource the nuances,” Ressa told Rappler, speaking about how AI is changing the newsroom.

But it’s not all doom and gloom. Ressa acknowledged that AI can have its place in the newsroom. Rappler, for example, has introduced an AI-driven summary on top of its stories to help readers quickly understand the news and context.
The lesson here is one of balance. While AI can certainly accelerate work, an overreliance on it can prevent people from developing the skills needed to actually accomplish their job.
“What happens to this next generation that doesn’t develop the skills that are necessary, to actually be able to pull up and think with clarity?” Ressa said.
“You can do it faster, but can you do it?” – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
articles.summary:
Pontiff delivers forceful speech on final day in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon

Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting…

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.

On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.
“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.
“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.

Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo greets a child while arriving on the popemobile to celebrate mass at the Villa Deportiva Regional Ucayali in Peru’s Amazon region. Photograph: Yara Nardi/Reuters

blocks.text: During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.

“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”
In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.
Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.
The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo XIV rides in helicopter cockpit with Peruvian air force pilots

blocks.text: Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.
His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.

“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”

The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.
In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.

articles.title: Pope visits Andes, Amazon in test of cancer recovery

articles.title: Snowbirds bid farewell to legendary jets in final flight over Calgary
articles.summary: The legendary CT-114 Tutor jets of the Canadian Forces Snowbirds took to the skies one last time over Calgary's McMahon Stadium Nov. 15, 2026, right before the 113th Grey Cup kicked off, setting the…

image.caption: The legendary CT-114 Tutor jets of the Canadian Forces Snowbirds took to the skies one last time over Calgary Nov. 15, 2026, right before the 113th Grey Cup kicked off, setting the stage for a dynamic match between the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes. (Michael King/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

The legendary CT-114 Tutor jets of the Canadian Forces Snowbirds took to the skies one last time over Calgary's McMahon Stadium Nov. 15, 2026, right before the 113th Grey Cup kicked off, setting the stage for a dynamic match between the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes.
CT-114 Tutor jets flew over McMahon Stadium for Grey Cup
The legendary jets of the Canadian Forces Snowbirds took to the skies one last time Sunday evening.

Smoke trailed behind the team's signature red-and-white CT-114 Tutor jets as they roared over Calgary's McMahon Stadium right before the 113th Grey Cup kicked off, setting the stage for a dynamic match between the Edmonton Elks and Montreal Alouettes.
In an interview with CBC News before the flight, Capt. Patrick Charette reflected on his time with the Snowbirds.
"Every good thing comes to an end," he said.
The Canadian Forces Snowbirds' CT-114 Tutor jets took to the skies one last time over Calgary's McMahon Stadium Nov. 15, 2026. (Amir Said/CBC)
The federal government announced in May that the CT-114 Tutor jets, which the CAF ordered as training aircraft in 1961, would be retired after the 2026 flying season.
"This is the end of this chapter for the Snowbirds, but we're proud and happy to be here in front of as many Canadians as posible, and we're excited for the future," Charette said.
Capt. Patrick Charette pictured in a file photo. This is his second season as a pilot with the Canadian Forces Snowbirds. (Cory Herperger/Radio-Canada)
The jets are set to be replaced by Swiss-made CT-157 Siskin II planes, but those won't be here until the 2030s at the earliest.
"We're excited for the future, coming back in a few years with the new aircraft and new team," Charette said.
"I can't imagine a more fitting occasion to do our last public display than the Grey Cup here in Calgary," he said

items: Snowbirds prepare to say goodbye to iconic 63-year-old jets in final airshow
A city between flights: How Moose Jaw is holding on to the Snowbirds

blocks.text: Aviation enthusiasts gathered across northwest Calgary to witness the squadron's last Tutor flyover.

"It's the only time I've really gotten to get a good look at them," said Ben Hunt, one of several plane spotters who gathered at the University of Calgary to watch the jets take their historic final flight.
"It's sad to see them go," he said.
The final flight of the Canadian Forces Snowbirds' CT-114 Tutor jets photographed from the University of Calgary on Nov. 15, 2026. (Michael King/CBC)
It was Jaime Garcia's third time seeing the Snowbirds in action.
"This is the last time unfortunately," he said. "Hopefully they come back stronger in a few years."
The Canadian Forces Snowbirds' CT-114 Tutor jets trailed their signature smoke as they roared over Calgary's McMahon Stadium for their last flight on Nov. 15, 2026. (Amir Said/CBC)
Garcia, an engineer who immigrated from Mexico, says the Snowbirds serve as an inspiration.
"Seeing them perform their tricks, and just seeing the skill and the talent of Canadian pilots, it inspires me," he said. "It makes me very happy to be in this country."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Amir Said is a multimedia journalist with CBC Calgary. He is an alumnus of the University of Regina, and his award-winning work as a writer and photographer has been published by outlets across Canada, including Postmedia, The Hill Times and The Narwhal. articles.title: Elon Musk joins 158,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
articles.summary:
Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’

Elon Musk and a host of…

blocks.text: Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.
The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to explain whether US national security had been put at risk – with some in the president’s own party suggesting that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌chief’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.

In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.
Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing.
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.

Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.

The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.

But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.
Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, according to officials, but not date has been set yet.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Huge waves pummel California coast, forcing closure of popular piers
articles.summary:
Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warning near coastal city

The California coast…

blocks.text: The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of popular piers.
The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.
“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said on social media.
On Saturday, waves above 50ft were recorded in San Mateo county, just south of San Francisco.
Surfers weren’t deterred, taking advantage of giant waves at the famous Mavericks beach near Half Moon Bay.
Farther south, the Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office issued an evacuation warning near the coastal town of Capitola that took the brunt of the powerful surf.

blocks.caption: Bystanders react after being caught in a sneaker wave near the Pacifica Pier in California on Saturday. Photograph: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/AP

blocks.text: In southern California, several piers, including ones in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego’s Pacific Beach, were closed during the weekend as they were slammed by waves.
At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, known for its lounging sea lions, water overflowed the beach and crashed up a staircase leading to the sand.
Conditions were calming by Sunday afternoon, but large waves were expected all week, forecasters warned.
The ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

articles.title: [New Rx] South Korea overcame its IMF crisis. Can Filipinos unite against inflation?
articles.summary: The Philippines can draw on South Korea's 1997 crisis recovery, and must replace external excuses with urgent domestic reforms, economic discipline, and collective action to overcome high inflation…

blocks.text: In 1997, South Korea faced economic collapse and required an International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout.
In an extraordinary display of solidarity, approximately 3.5 million Koreans donated jewelry and wedding rings, collecting over 220 tonnes of gold to help secure foreign currency.
Combined with sweeping reforms, Korea rebounded from a 5.8% contraction in 1998 to approximately 10% growth in 1999. By August 2001, it had repaid its IMF loans ahead of schedule.
Korea’s recovery required government leadership, economic discipline, and collective sacrifice.
Nearly three decades later, the Philippines faces a different challenge. But the lesson remains relevant.

October 2026 inflation reached 7.8% in the Philippines, compared with 5.1% in Vietnam, 3.9% in Thailand, and 3.2% in Indonesia. Thailand’s inflation was itself a 45-month high, driven largely by energy costs. Yet Philippine inflation was twice as high.

Growth offers little comfort. Philippine GDP expanded just 2.4% in the second quarter, against 8.4% in Vietnam, 6.0% in Malaysia, and 5.9% in Singapore. Worse, newly released figures show Philippine growth slowing further to 2.1% in the third quarter.
Figure 1. Inflation across major ASEAN economies – Year-on-year CPI inflation · October 2026, except September for Singapore and Malaysia
Figure 2. GDP growth across major ASEAN economies – Q2 2026 · Year-on-year real GDP growth
For a developing economy needing higher incomes and better infrastructure, this combination is alarming.
The peso recently breached ₱64 per US dollar before recovering slightly, increasing import costs and currency risks.
And El Niño’s full economic consequences may still lie ahead.
PAGASA expects the very strong event to persist into the first half of 2027. Gandara, Samar, has already declared a state of calamity amid drought and water shortages.

Only months ago, parts of the Philippines faced severe floods. Now communities struggle to secure water. Existing reservoirs and irrigation systems must be better maintained and coordinated to store wet-season water for dry-season use.
Poor water management becomes an inflation problem when harvests fall and food prices rise.
Global shocks may be unavoidable. Domestic inefficiency is not.
During COVID-19, government, businesses, and citizens rapidly adapted. Remote work expanded, operations changed, and agencies coordinated responses.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. should bring comparable urgency today. The Inter-Agency Committee on Inflation and Market Outlook, established in 2023, should become a presidentially supervised task force coordinating transportation, energy, agriculture, finance, and infrastructure.
Its mandate should extend beyond monitoring prices and distributing subsidies: remove avoidable costs, repair irrigation, address logistical bottlenecks, and publish measurable results.
Interest-rate adjustments alone cannot accomplish these reforms.
Metro Manila, Cebu, and Davao could introduce rotating conservation days by business district or government office.
Suitable employees would work remotely, meetings would move online, and nonessential travel would decline. Essential services, manufacturing, freight, and public transportation would continue.
This is not another lockdown. It is an effort to save fuel, electricity, water, and commuting hours.

Life expectancy in the Philippines is approximately 70 years, compared with 84 in South Korea and 83 in Singapore. Yet someone commuting two to three hours each workday could spend 2.3–3.4 entire years traveling over a 40-year career.
Why sacrifice so much precious time?
Employers should expand remote work. Professionals heading to the same district could carpool and conduct discussions during shared commutes.
Consider requiring three occupants, including the driver, in private vehicles on designated roads during peak hours, with sensible exemptions.
Grab should encourage pooled rides through discounts, with higher peak-hour pricing for exclusive trips subject to regulation.

Politicians should reduce convoys. EDSA and C5 should progressively transition from jeepneys on trunk routes to high-capacity city buses with numbered routes, fixed stops, and reliable schedules. Existing operators should have opportunities in bus services and feeder routes.
Political and religious gatherings should avoid unnecessarily obstructing main roads while respecting freedom of assembly.
Inflation does not end at the supermarket checkout. It also erodes whatever Filipinos manage to save.
Consider ₱100,000 earning 3% annual interest. After the government’s 20% withholding tax on interest, the household receives just ₱2,400. Even at 4% inflation, its purchasing power declines.
The government collects tax on nominal earnings that fail to preserve the household’s wealth.
Singapore generally exempts individual interest income from deposits with approved banks.
The Philippines should exempt the first ₱10,000 of annual bank deposit interest from withholding tax, helping ordinary savers build emergency reserves. Larger interest earnings could remain taxable.
As El Niño threatens household budgets, encouraging financial preparedness should become part of economic policy.
Prepare, conserve, and spend modestly
Thai retailers report increased purchases of essentials despite inflation being only half the Philippine rate. Filipinos should prepare sensibly without hoarding.
Christmas also offers an opportunity for discipline.
Government agencies, companies, and professional organizations should hold joint celebrations, sharing venues, catering, and transportation instead of staging separate costly events.
Households can celebrate modestly, avoid unnecessary borrowing, and prioritize savings.
Those with greater resources should shoulder greater responsibility, while lower-income households need affordable alternatives.
Korea demonstrated what reforms and public participation can achieve together.

Filipinos have long taken pride in their resilience. But resilience should mean more than enduring hardship. It should translate into practical measures that strengthen the economy and protect household purchasing power.

Government must provide leadership and implement meaningful reforms. Businesses should improve efficiency and reduce unnecessary costs. Households should be encouraged to conserve resources, spend prudently, and build savings. – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is a physician, healthcare investor, and adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines Manila. He writes about healthcare economics, investment, and public policy in the Philippines and across Asia.

articles.title: Coles investigating ‘cybersecurity incident’ and apologises to customers
articles.summary:
Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data breached in cyber-attack but recommends customers update passwords

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.
Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating the incident with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts.
“Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange.
“We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems.
“Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.”
Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”.
“We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said.
“We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.”
Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they receive unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links.
More details soon …

articles.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
articles.summary: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByVitaly Shevchenko
Chief Analyst, BBC Monitoring

blocks.caption: Vitaly Shevchenko

blocks.text: Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.
Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.
"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."
In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The silence of Russian businessmen at a Kremlin summit with Putin in 2022 perhaps demonstrated their fear of the president

blocks.text: Image source, ALEXEY NIKOLSKY/SPUTNIK/AFP via Getty Images
The silence of Russian businessmen at a Kremlin summit with Putin in 2022 perhaps demonstrated their fear of the president
And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.
Restless tycoons

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule". They had money, which back then meant power.

This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.

But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some oligarchs developed a distinctive dress sense in the 1990s, as later satirised by this St Petersburg artist

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Some oligarchs developed a distinctive dress sense in the 1990s, as later satirised by this St Petersburg artist

Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.

"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.

Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).
But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.
Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy?
Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.
"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."
And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.

"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.
And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.

There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."

blocks.caption: Image caption, One prominent oligarch of the 1990s was Boris Berezovsky, who fell out with the Kremlin and lived his later years in the UK

blocks.text: Image source, CARL DE SOUZA/AFP via Getty Images
One prominent oligarch of the 1990s was Boris Berezovsky, who fell out with the Kremlin and lived his later years in the UK

If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.
In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.

Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.

Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.

And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.

This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.

Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.
Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine

blocks.text: Image source, Vladimir Smirnov SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPA/Shutterstock
Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine

He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.

Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.
Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.

But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.
A bombshell interview
An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.

Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.

In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.

But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.
Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says.

The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.

Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.
No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some tycoons feel ostracised because of Western sanctions, unable to fly private jets and visit Western resorts like Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in southern France, which used to be popular with rich Russians

blocks.text: Image source, Andrey Rudakov/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Some tycoons feel ostracised because of Western sanctions, unable to fly private jets and visit Western resorts like Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in southern France, which used to be popular with rich Russians

Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.

Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future".
But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.

Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man."

Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen."

Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

articles.title: Digital finance products used to abuse almost 20% of young women and girls, UK report finds
articles.summary:
Survey respondents describe current or former partners controlling bank accounts and taking out credit online without full consent

Almost one in five young women and girls in the UK have…

blocks.text: Almost one in five young women and girls in the UK have experienced digital financial products being used as a tool of abuse by a current or former partner, a report has found.

Abusers are exploiting banking apps, online payments and digital credit to control young women, causing financial harm and preventing them from leaving relationships, according to research from the charity Surviving Economic Abuse.
Research for a new report from the charity, Access Denied, Futures Derailed, involved carrying out a nationally representative survey of young women and teenage girls, with Ipsos UK.

It found that almost one in five teenage girls and young women aged 16-24 in the UK – equivalent to nearly 700,000 people – had been affected by this form of abuse. One in three young women experience economic abuse. Rates are highest among disabled young women and those with caring responsibilities for children, with perpetrators exploiting additional vulnerabilities to exert control.

The research found that one in eight girls and young women had experienced a current or ex-partner preventing them from having login information, such as passwords for online banking, while the same number had experienced an abuser controlling their digital wallets.
It also found 7% of respondents had experienced an abuser taking out credit in their name without their consent or because they were scared to refuse, including from “buy now, pay later” lenders.

More than 40% of those who had experienced abuse said it had caused them financial difficulty, while half said it had had a negative impact on their mental health, such as anxiety, depression, panic attacks, self-harm or suicidal thoughts.

More than a third said the economic abuse prevented them from leaving a relationship with the abuser, and one in six had had to borrow money, including from digital lenders such as “buy now, pay later” and online payday lenders, to cover essential items or bills.

Becky* met her now ex-partner when she was 18 and was trapped in a relationship with him for more than a decade, during which time he isolated her from her family and friends, coerced her into more than £40,000 of debt, and prevented her from working.

Even though she fled nearly seven years ago, she continues to live with the impact of his abuse to this day. “I had good credit at the time and he didn’t,” she said. “Even though I said no, he broke me down over many months and forced me to take out a loan in my name to pay for a holiday that he wanted to go on.”

She said that he also obtained “buy now, pay later” loans in her name, which she only found out about when letters came through the post. “There was no verification, it seemed like all he needed from my address and date of birth,” she said, adding that when she left the relationship, the interest on the debt “was huge”.
“I had to access an [individual voluntary arrangement] but this destroyed my credit score,” she said. “When I fled, it was a huge struggle. I couldn’t get a phone or wifi.”

As it was her first proper relationship, she said she “didn’t know what was healthy or not healthy”, adding: “He also isolated me from my family and friends, so I had no one to reach out to. I wish that the government would make sure there is education about economic abuse in schools and in colleges.
“We also need to see banks building in extra layers of protection, particularly with the rising use of AI, they need to be responding to evolving perpetrator tactics.”
after newsletter promotion

Experts and survivors are calling on ministers to use its promised financial education curriculum to educate young people about economic abuse. They are also asking financial services to remove opportunities for domestic abusers to exploit digital financial products and create additional protections to support survivors, including when adopting AI into their systems and processes.
Sam Smethers, the chief executive of Surviving Economic Abuse, said digital financial products could be “weapons of abuse”.
“To halve violence against women and girls, we must tackle abuse where it happens, including through the digital financial products young women use every day,” she added.

“We also want to see financial services firms working with survivors and experts to design out abuse of digital financial products and build in protections. Without action, we risk leaving hundreds of thousands of young women to pay the price.”

The minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Satvir Kaur, said: “This report shines an important light on a type of abuse that too often goes unrecognised and can take many forms, from controlling someone’s money, to their choices, to their future.”

“This government has set the unprecedented ambition to halve violence against women and girls in a decade,” Kaur added. “Through our ‘Enough’ campaign, we are working with partners across society, including the banking sector, to help people recognise the signs of economic abuse, challenge abusive behaviour and support victims to access the help they need and deserve.”
*Name has been changed

items: In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org

articles.title: ‘Loaded with potential’: stage version of TV smash It’s a Sin has the dancefloor at its heart
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Trailer released for Rambert’s version of Russell T Davies’s show about friendship amid the 80s Aids crisis and the ‘extraordinary freedom’ of clubbing

Russell T…

blocks.text: Russell T Davies’s award-winning series It’s a Sin, about young gay friends living through the Aids crisis in 1980s London, is getting a new life as a dance piece, with a trailer released on Monday ahead of an opening at Aviva Studios in Manchester in February.

“We had a few approaches, but a lot of people wanted to make it a musical, which made my heart sink slightly,” said Davies. “I always imagined an aria between those two women on the seafront at the end and I thought: ‘Oh, that could be so terrible!’” Dance was different, he said. “It felt so original and so pure. The story distils down to these emotional moments that are going to be done so beautifully on stage.”

The idea came from Benoit Swan Pouffer, artistic director of Rambert, which celebrated its centenary this year with a commitment to bringing in new audiences, in part by reinventing familiar titles, as in its dance version of Peaky Blinders. “Dance needs to be democratised and this is the way to do it,” said Pouffer, who is choreographing It’s a Sin.

Davies has a cameo in the trailer, although his own dance career peaked with a performance for Princess Diana with West Glamorgan youth theatre (she told him he should continue to “Dance, dance, dance!”). The dancefloor, however, has always been an inspiration. “They’re such potent places, so loaded with potential.” Davies spent many nights in the clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, watching lives play out to music. “Those dancefloors were places of such extraordinary freedom,” he said. “Especially in the 80s, with that layer of secrecy. That’s where you’d be out – you might not be out at home – becoming the person you aspired to be.”

blocks.caption: It’s a Sin trailer in full.

blocks.text: The dance world was notably affected by the Aids epidemic. “I had friends and colleagues who left us too early,” said Pouffer. He was dancing in the US in the mid-90s, and saw as much stigma about HIV and Aids in the dance world as anywhere else. “There was shame, it was hidden. Even Alvin Ailey, that’s not what we said [that he died of an Aids-related illness] when he passed. Even now there is still a stigma,” said Pouffer. “The trauma, you put it in a little capsule and you don’t talk about it. Now we have this young PrEP generation who don’t know how traumatic it was. The closest they can think of is Covid,” he suggested. “Remember in the beginning when we didn’t know anything about the virus?”

Pouffer also wants to convey the excitement and creative spark of the era. “The fashion, the music, the dance of the 80s, it was one of the peaks of history,” he said. There will be video and narration to help tell the story, with scripts by Kaite O’Reilly. Davies is an executive producer, as are Pet Shop Boys, whose title song will feature alongside an original soundtrack by Roman GianArthur.

blocks.caption: Rambert’s Benoit Swan Pouffer, centre, with (l-r) dancers Dipesh Verma, Naya Lovell, Archie White and Dylan Tedaldi. Photograph: Rambert/STEAM

blocks.text: When Davies originally pitched the TV series he was turned down by all the major UK networks, even Channel 4, which eventually commissioned it. “It was simply an assumption that it would be miserable, even when they had the first script to read,” he said.

The series went on to be a huge hit. “Not a week goes past without someone stopping me in the street,” said Davies. Yet it was hard to celebrate, “because no matter how proud we were, it’s a story that’s founded on a lot of deaths”.

There is “a great heaviness at the heart of it, a great sadness and loss,” he continued. “But we told it with joy and vigour and life. The most important thing is to remember the life that those people had, not the death … I think the show worked because it turned around and said: ‘Hey, we loved those boys. Remember the love.’”

items: It’s a Sin is on tour from 16 February to 13 November 2027

articles.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
articles.summary: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.

blocks.text: Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.
Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.

Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.
At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.
The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.

He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.
At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.
At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo influenced Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.

items: How one DEA killing began a brutal war

blocks.text: In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.
Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.
His death sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.
In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was placed under house arrest since 2022 and died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.
In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.
From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.
In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.

articles.title: ASEAN opens ‘progress-based’ path for Myanmar’s return, but keeps restrictions
articles.summary: ‘We want to see how Myanmar responds,’ says Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, as ASEAN weighs restoring Myanmar’s political representation based on its adherence to the bloc’s peace…

blocks.text: RETREAT. Leaders and representatives gather for the 49th ASEAN Summit retreat session at the Coconut Palace in Pasay City on November 15, 2026.
ASEAN Philippines 2026

‘We want to see how Myanmar responds,’ says Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, as ASEAN weighs restoring Myanmar’s political representation based on its adherence to the bloc’s peace plan

items: ASEAN leaders have opened the possibility for Myanmar's political representatives to gradually return to high-level meetings, contingent on Myanmar's progress in implementing the Five-Point Consensus.
The approach will be phased and progress-based, with ASEAN expressing deep concern over the insufficient progress made by Myanmar so far.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have opened a path to a possible “step-by-step” return of Myanmar’s political representatives to high-level meetings, although this remains conditional on Myanmar demonstrating concrete progress in implementing the bloc’s peace plan.

In their review and decision on the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus (5PC), ASEAN leaders agreed to pursue “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar through a “phased and progress-based approach.”

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” said the document adopted on Sunday, November 15, the first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila.
In the same document, ASEAN leaders also reitered their “deep concern over the insufficient progress in the implementation of the 5PC.”

The regional bloc has previously left the door open for Myanmar’s political return. But the decision makes the possibility of a gradual restoration more explicit, even as leaders maintained existing restrictions.

In 2021, Myanmar’s military launched a coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged the country into a bloody civil war. Since then, ASEAN has barred Myanmar’s political leaders from attending ASEAN summits and foreign ministers’ meetings, allowing only non-political representatives to participate.

blocks.caption: Rappler Recap: Myanmar, South China Sea among issues as 49th ASEAN Summit opens

blocks.text: The decision comes amid calls from some member countries, particularly Thailand, to re-engage Myanmar’s military-backed government following elections held under military rule. The elections remain contentious, however, with ASEAN leaders only saying they “noted the conclusion of the three phases of Myanmar’s general elections,” without explicitly endorsing its validity.

Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who also serves as ASEAN’s special envoy on Myanmar, explained that the step-by-step approach would depend on whether Myanmar follows the peace plan.
“The step-by-step approach is adherence to the Five-Point Consensus. So, for example, the first one is cessation of hostilities,” Lazaro said in a press briefing on Sunday evening.

“We want to see how Myanmar responds to that because right now, there’s still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people. So step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we monitor that,” she added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'I cheated': South Korean admits he used AI to achieve top score in national exam
articles.summary: The marks attained by the top scorer on South Korea's national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true, and on ‌Sunday, skeptics were proven right when he confessed to…

image.caption: A classroom is seen prior to an exam in Marseille, France, on June 11. A man in South Korea admitted on Sunday that he cheated using AI to achieve his top score in a national exam for aspiring tax accountants. (Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The marks attained by the top scorer on South Korea's national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true, and on ‌Sunday, skeptics were proven right when he confessed to using generative AI to cheat.
Revelation prompts 'countermeasures' from officials ahead of college entrance exams

The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams taken in April and July. ​It has also raised the stakes for organizers of ​South Korea's high-stakes annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

"I cheated using electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the ​top score was not the result of fair effort," he said, ⁠identifying himself by the ⁠surname Han, as he apologized on the ‌YouTube channel Attorney Lee Don-ho.
Han said he cheated by taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an artificial intelligence tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
Speaking on camera wearing a face ⁠mask, Han added that he had submitted a written confession to Seoul police.
Can Canadian universities stop students from using AI to cheat?
A Reuters call to the Seoul Jungbu police station went unanswered on Sunday.
The scandal has rattled a ‌country where standardized tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories, coming just four days ahead of Thursday's annual national college entrance exam.

items: AI cheating runs wild on campus

blocks.text: "The presidential office views the matter very seriously, and because the college entrance exam is next ​week, we have been working hard to prepare countermeasures," a senior presidential office official told reporters on Sunday.

The official ⁠said that reports of potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam were ⁠concerning, adding that the presidential chief of staff for policy would convene an emergency ⁠meeting ⁠later in the afternoon to ​address the issue.
Students wait for the start of the annual college entrance examinations in a Seoul classroom in November 2025. (Kim Hong-ji/The Associated Press)

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook acknowledged on Friday public concerns over AI-assisted cheating ahead ​of the national college entrance ⁠exam, a high-pressure event that many South Korean students have spent much of their lives preparing for.

The government "will prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably," a statement ⁠from her office said.

articles.title: Yemen: Anti-Houthi forces pull back as rebels advance
articles.summary: Forces aligned with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia are seeking to strengthen control over the interim capital Aden as the Iran-backed Houthis approach.

image.caption: The fighting in Yemen has been going on for years, with Saudi Arabia and Iran supporting opposing sidesImage: Mohammed Al-Wafi/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Southern Armed Forces group allied with Yemen's UN-recognized government and backed by Saudi Arabia said Sunday they had repositioned themselves away from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Why are troops moving away from Bab el-Mandeb?

The Southern Armed Forces said the repositioning is intended to secure the southern city of Aden, "and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the frontlines and addressing existing threats."
Aden, which has a population of over a million people, is the interim seat of the Yemeni government, formally known as the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC).
The Southern Armed Forces also intend to end the Houthi siege over the strategic southwestern city of Taiz.
Nearly two million people live in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city.
The siege is raising fears of famine for residents, as well as a possible medical crisis as hospitals face restricted supplies.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
Houthis advancing towards Aden
The Houthis control much of northwest Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
The rebels are a Shiite militant group backed by Iran. The US, Canada and several other countries regard them as a terror organization.
The Houthis in September launched a rapid offensive against the PLC, seizing much of the coastline along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
It is also a key corridor for maritime trade and energy shipments.
The Houthis have taken control of the major port town of Mocha in September, firming their grip over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The latest redeployment of the Southern Armed Forces is likely to give the rebels even more control over the strategic area.
Sources told AFP news agency that Houthi forces are now just 60 kilometers (less than 40 miles) from Aden.
The conflict between the Yemeni government and the Houthis has lasted for over 10 years.
The fighting in Yemen, the poorest country in the Arab world, has been fueled by the wider rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia.
More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia

In recent weeks, the Houthis have been launching frequent attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sunday, the rebels claimed that they targeted the King Khalid International Airport and financial district of the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the alleged Houthi attack.
