articles.title: US officials recover audio from ‘Mississippi miracle’ cruise ship and tanker crash
articles.summary:
Tank vessel suffered sudden steering failure two minutes before slamming into docked riverboat near New Orleans

Federal safety investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board…

blocks.text: Federal safety investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) recovered audio and released a preliminary timeline on Sunday of a collision between a cruise ship and a tanker vessel in the Mississippi River on Friday.

The data was retrieved after more than 30 people were injured when a tanker collided with a docked cruise ship – American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage riverboat – near the port of New Orleans on Friday at about 12.30pm. All passengers aboard the cruise ship have been accounted for, officials said.
The tank vessel suffered a sudden steering failure two minutes before slamming into the docked riverboat, causing it to tip on to its side, officials said.

“It experienced the steering casualty, resulting in the rudder remaining to starboard,” said Bart Barnum, senior marine accident investigator for the NTSB’s office of marine safety, during a media briefing on Sunday. “Following the steering casualty, the Atlantic Asphalt veered to starboard toward the east bank of the river.”

Before the collision, audio collected by officials captured “the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance broadcasted over the vessel’s marine radio, commands to deploy the vessel’s anchors, and emergency ship handling orders”, according to Barnum.
The NTSB is leading the safety investigation alongside the US Coast Guard, as well as American Cruise Lines and representatives from the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the tanker’s flag state.
A preliminary report is expected to be published within 30 days.

Images and videos of the collision have been circulating online. The father of a cruise ship worker who survived the collision spoke about the moment his daughter called him in the middle of the incident.

“She’s FaceTiming me hysterically in a lifejacket in the middle of the Mississippi River crying, ‘Dad, dad, I had to jump off the boat,’” said Wayne Hager in an interview with Good Morning America over the weekend. “I’m hearing people screaming and yelling in the background and kind of like some, I don’t know, like metal grinding noises or whatever.”

blocks.caption: Emergency personnel and crews work the scene after a tanker crashed into a river cruise ship in New Orleans on Friday. Photograph: Enan Chediak/The Times-Picayune/AP

blocks.text: Video of Leelah Hager posted on social media later shows her in the water wearing a life vest immediately after the collision between the Atlantic Asphalt tanker and the cruise ship, which had about 190 passengers and crew aboard. Other images of the incident show how the tanker caused the American Heritage to capsize.

New Orleans port officials filed a lawsuit seeking more than $1m in damages from the owner and operator of the asphalt tanker. Four crew members of the American Heritage filed a separate lawsuit against Nave Shipping and Thome Ship Management, which oversee the tanker, claiming they “suffered significant and life changing injuries to their mind and body”, according to the suit.

According to the document, the collision caused the cruise ship to partially sink, throwing the crew members and passengers of the American Heritage “overboard into the Mississippi River, not knowing if they were going to live or die”, the lawsuit reads.
The crew members of American Heritage are alleging negligence, gross negligence, carelessness or fault of the managers of the tanker.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] ASEAN digital deal needs a Philippine dividend
articles.summary: Easier commercial transactions are the real test through which ASEAN’s diplomatic achievement on DEFA must eventually enter the Philippine economy

blocks.text: ASEAN’s new digital trade pact promises smoother cross-border commerce, yet the real test for Manila lies in proving that local merchants, exporters, and consumers actually capture the financial gains. To turn diplomatic momentum into measurable economic dividends, the Philippine government must close the treaty scrutiny gap, track hard commercial benchmarks, and address foundational infrastructure bottlenecks before declaring victory.

The Philippines has helped deliver a regional digital agreement, but its harder assignment is proving that a Filipino merchant will pay less to collect an overseas sale, an exporter will clear documents faster, and a consumer cheated across borders will have somewhere effective to turn.
Those everyday commercial transactions are the real test through which ASEAN’s diplomatic achievement must eventually enter the Philippine economy.
Economic ministers signed the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, or DEFA, in Manila on Saturday, November 14, ahead of the leaders’ summit, a milestone confirmed by the ASEAN Secretariat.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] ASEAN digital deal needs a Philippine dividend

blocks.text: Signing gives participating governments a concrete diplomatic achievement to claim, yet businesses still need clarity on when specific obligations become effective, what domestic rules must change, and how compliance will be enforced across borders.

Singapore’s official factsheet describes DEFA as a legally binding agreement covering digital trade, cross-border payments, data protection, competition, and cybersecurity. According to the factsheet, the agreement enters into force 180 days after signing, with the full legal text scheduled for publication on ASEAN’s website in early 2027. That publication timetable leaves an immediate scrutiny gap.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Singapore Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry

blocks.text: Before endorsing sweeping claims about investor protection or regulatory constraints, businesses, legal analysts, and lawmakers need to examine the actual provisions, national exceptions, and dispute settlement mechanisms.

Still, the underlying economic case deserves a fair hearing. Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong acknowledged during the rollout that ASEAN member-states negotiated from vastly different levels of digital readiness, identifying interoperable payments, digital identities, and electronic trade documents among priority implementation projects. Making national systems work together could spare a small exporter the recurring expense of repeatedly proving its identity, reproducing physical paperwork, or arranging separate payment channels for each regional market.

Consider a Philippine manufacturer selling specialty food products to a regional distributor. Electronic customs and trade documentation could cut administrative overhead, while faster cross-border settlement could shorten the lag between shipping an order and receiving cash.

That efficiency would improve working capital without forcing the business to take on additional debt. This scenario illustrates the agreement’s potential benefit, however, rather than proving that DEFA has already delivered those savings.

To avoid confusion between diplomatic promise and commercial reality, the Philippine government should establish a clear baseline before claiming an economic dividend. Agencies should measure the total cost of receiving a cross-border payment—including foreign-exchange spreads and intermediary fees—alongside document rejection rates, average settlement times, and the number of smaller firms completing repeat export orders.

Publishing these benchmarks regularly will matter. A digital trade pact earns economic credibility only when businesses can identify which expense disappeared and how much cash they retained. Industry groups should help select those indicators so the scorecard reflects genuine commercial experience; otherwise, agencies risk counting websites launched, meetings held, and memoranda signed while leaving the cost of trading across borders unchanged for smaller firms.

Investors should likewise ask who ultimately captures the efficiency gains. A payment provider or digital platform could gain customers and transaction volume while merchants see little reduction in fees.

Alternatively, seamless connections between providers could intensify competition and force transaction charges down. Neither outcome follows automatically from the signing ceremony. Valuing banks, fintech firms, or logistics operators on the assumption of an immediate regional windfall would run well ahead of demonstrated implementation and commercial results.

Consumer protection belongs squarely inside that calculation. If a cross-border transaction fails or turns fraudulent, the customer needs to know which institution must investigate, what digital evidence can be obtained, and who carries the financial loss. Policymakers should explain how Philippine regulators will cooperate with foreign counterparts, preserve access to transaction records, and resolve cross-border complaints.
Raising these questions is part of sound implementation and treaty scrutiny, not an argument that the agreement has weakened existing domestic safeguards.

At the same time, there is a legitimate objection to excessive regulatory caution: fragmented national requirements often insulate established incumbents and make regional expansion prohibitively expensive for smaller competitors. Preserving every local procedure intact would defeat the purpose of integration.

The practical answer is to distinguish essential consumer and security safeguards from duplicative compliance, then demonstrate that the resulting framework preserves clear accountability. Easier transactions and effective supervision must be designed together, with institutional responsibilities settled before customers encounter a problem.

Financing is beginning to accompany the policy commitments. On Saturday, the Asian Development Bank announced that its regional platform for artificial intelligence and the digital economy aims to mobilize up to US$5 billion in public and private financing by 2030 to support DEFA implementation across infrastructure, payments, digital identification, cybersecurity, and related reforms. Importantly, this represents a multi-year financing target across the entire region, not US$5 billion already disbursed or earmarked for the Philippines.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] ASEAN digital deal needs a Philippine dividend

blocks.text: For Manila, the next useful disclosure is a concrete project pipeline identifying Philippine beneficiaries, financing terms, lead implementing agencies, and target completion dates. A broad regional envelope tells investors little about which domestic bottlenecks will actually be removed.

Project preparation also matters: an attractive headline figure cannot substitute for disciplined procurement, technical capacity, and clear accountability when delivery slips. Any public borrowing tied to digital infrastructure must be judged against measurable productivity gains and ongoing operating costs.

The Philippines must also resist treating regional digital rules as a substitute for domestic competitiveness. An exporter still relies on dependable broadband connectivity, reliable electricity, and efficient physical logistics, alongside workers trained to operate digital systems.

If those foundational constraints remain unresolved, regional integration could make it easier for better-prepared foreign competitors to serve Philippine consumers than for Philippine firms to expand abroad—a risk that must be tested against actual investment and export data.

Ultimately, DEFA gives the Philippine ASEAN chairship a substantive policy result, and dismissing it as mere ceremony would ignore the real value of lowering regional barriers. The administration should now publish its agency implementation responsibilities, explain the treaty’s legal safeguards once the text is released, and commit to tracking hard business outcomes.

The strongest claim Manila could eventually make is straightforward: Philippine firms kept more of every sale, reached more regional customers, and recovered their money when something went wrong. Until that evidence arrives, the signing remains a promising achievement awaiting its economic accounting. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Steering casualty' preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
articles.summary: Preliminary findings by National Transportation Safety Board investigators suggest the tanker suffered a steering failure before colliding with the cruise ship on Friday.

blocks.text: The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.
Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.

"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.
The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.
A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.
Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.
Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.
The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

articles.title: Police ban protests near 10 schools and five universities in Paris
articles.summary: The order will be in place from 16 to 20 November, Paris police chief Patrice Faure says.

blocks.text: Police in Paris have issued a five-day ban on protests near 10 secondary schools and five universities as authorities try to control weeks of blockades and violence at educational venues in France.
The order prohibits unauthorised gatherings or marches within 100m of the sites from 16 to 20 November.

Paris police chief Patrice Faure said the ban was necessary due to "numerous disruptions and blockades around certain secondary schools and establishments of higher learning" and "persistent violence".
A wave of protests began in France September over poor secondary school conditions, before spreading to universities, workers and a "yellow-vest" movement against the cost of living.

Announcing the order, the Paris police chief said blockades around certain secondary schools and universities have led to damaged public property, violence against members of the educational community and clashes with law enforcement.
Mayors of eight Parisian districts had contacted the regional education authority to call for measures to "secure the entrances and exits" of blockaded secondary schools, local media report.
Some 1,548 people have been arrested in Paris since the start of the protests, Faure said on Sunday.

articles.title: Prince Harry tells Ukrainians they are ‘going to win war’ on surprise trip to Lviv
articles.summary:
Duke of Sussex meets wounded veterans in city and says country could one day host Invictus Games

Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a…

blocks.text: Prince Harry has told Ukrainian soldiers they are going to win the war with Russia, during a surprise visit to the country.

The Duke of Sussex met wounded veterans and medics in the city of Lviv, in the west of Ukraine, as he addressed a conference on treating those injured in war. He said he had taken a risk in travelling to the country, but that he had felt “warmth” when arriving on Saturday.
It is the British army veteran’s fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia’s invasion in February 2022.

He spoke at a conference organised by the Superhumans Center, a clinic in Lviv that specialises in care and rehabilitation of those who have fought in the conflict. The prince has previously supported the group, which provides prosthetic limbs to those who have lost them in battle.
He said: “Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success.”

blocks.caption: Harry speaking to Valery Odainyk, a Ukrainian veteran and wheelchair rugby player who competed in last year’s Invictus Games. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: Harry watched wheelchair rugby players who hope to be in Ukraine’s team at next year’s Invictus Games, which will take place in Birmingham. Ukraine is aiming to send about 60 competitors to the event – its largest ever team.

The prince said the games for wounded military veterans, which he set up in 2014, could one day be held in Ukraine. “When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” he promised.

At the rugby match, Harry hugged a player he recognised – Valery Odainyk, who took part in the Invictus Games in Canada in 2025. The 41-year-old, who uses prosthetic legs, said he was “still an active serviceman”, and the prince expressed surprise he found time to train.
Odainyk said afterwards he had told Harry his involvement in his sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games”.
after newsletter promotion

The prince visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, in September 2025 and in April this year. During the April visit, he called Ukraine “a country bravely and successfully defending Europe’s eastern flank” and said “it matters that we don’t lose sight of the significance of that”.
The 42-year-old spent a decade in the British army and served in Afghanistan, including as a helicopter pilot. He has described those years as the happiest of his life.

articles.title: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
articles.summary: He has been showing support for injured veterans in Ukraine and praising the country's resilience.

blocks.text: That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.

In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.
He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".
"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.
"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.
At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.
He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.
In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.
And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."
Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.
"Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth, I feel encouragement," he said, having returned for a fourth trip here during wartime.
He promised that "when the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games".
There have been 400 wounded service men and women in Ukraine taking part in trials for next year's games, being hosted in Birmingham.
The sports events are an attempt to encourage rehabilitation and to recognise the resilience of people overcoming their challenges.
Prince Harry told a gathering of new Invictus members of a "cultural shift" from people being socially awkward about seeing injured veterans to wanting to show respect.
"These people have so much to offer," he said.

"Recovery cannot wait for the war to end, The scale of need in Ukraine is huge, and wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans need the chance to rebuild their lives now," said Rob Owen, chief executive officer of the Invictus Games Foundation.

articles.title: Australia, UK, Canada and Italy urge Israel to allow critical aid to Gaza ahead of winter
articles.summary:
Four countries call situation ‘entirely reversible’ in joint statement as flooding exacerbates humanitarian crisis

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and Italy have urged Israel to allow critical humanitarian aid to enter Gaza, describing the situation on the ground as “dire”.
The four countries released a joint statement on Monday morning, urging Israel to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies being held at the border into Gaza ahead of winter.
“We, the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom, are clear that as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire,” the statement said.
“The recent floods have brought further suffering – and this was only the first storm of the winter. People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance.”
The ministers said Israel has time to act “before the winter fully sets in”.

“This situation is entirely reversible … we today urge the government of Israel to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza,” the foreign ministers said.
“The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.”

Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents after deadly storms in the past week. Thousands more have been left without shelter while sanitation infrastructure has also been destroyed by storms.
At least four Palestinian children and woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents.
Australia’s Greens leader and foreign affairs spokesperson, David Shoebridge, said “harsh words” from the government would do little, and that the government should instead take more concrete action.

“The Israeli Government has not responded to harsh words from Australia before, they won’t now. Material action, sanctions on the war cabinet, ending the two-way arms trade, implementing sanctions on illegal settlements as other nations have done. These are real actions the Albanese Government can take but has failed to,” Shoebridge said.
Shoebridge said Australia previously refused to join commitments by multiple allies including the UK that called for import bans on trade from illegal Israeli settlements.
“When it was a statement committing to material action, Australia disappeared,” Shoebridge said.

The foreign ministers urged all parties to implement the comprehensive plan for Gaza, respect the ceasefire and “their obligations under international humanitarian law, and allowing aid to reach the people who need it.”
On Monday, Australian cabinet minister Madeleine King told ABC radio the four nations had worked on the statement.

“This particular group has been working on this kind of statement for a little while to make sure that people that are affected by the war in the Middle East can receive the assistance they need,” she said.
“But, really importantly … is the fact that this humanitarian aid will be able to be delivered.”

articles.title: Somali-American Uber driver brutally assaulted in alleged hate crime in Minnesota
articles.summary:
Mohamed Yusuf is fighting for his life after alleged attack by passenger who said he did not like driver’s first name

A Somali-American Uber driver was allegedly brutally assaulted by a…

blocks.text: A Somali-American Uber driver was allegedly brutally assaulted by a passenger in Hopkins, Minnesota, on Saturday, in what his family says “appears to be a hate crime”.

The driver, Mohamed Yusuf, is currently hospitalized and fighting for his life, his family told the Somali Brief, a digital news site run by two Somali American journalists. The driver’s cousin, Abdinasir Ali told the outlet that the alleged attack took place early Saturday after a passenger in Hopkins, a suburban city south-west of Minneapolis, asked Yusuf’s name and then said he did not like the name Mohamed.

The passenger allegedly then choked the driver from behind, took control of the car and used it to assault the driver. “He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle,” Yusuf’s son, Mustafa Osman, told the Somali Brief.
The badly injured driver was later found “a mile down the road in a ditch”, with broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs and a spinal injury, his son said.
The Hopkins police department said in a statement they are investigating the assault after officers responded to a report of a suspicious vehicle at 1.20am on Saturday.

“Officers located an adult male suspect nearby and took him into custody,” the police department stated. They noted preliminary information indicates the incident involved an Uber ride share interaction and that the investigation remains ongoing.
“This is a pure hate crime,” one member of Yusuf’s family at the hospital told the Somali Brief. “Our politicians created this hostile environment.”

The alleged assault comes after Donald Trump made racist rhetoric and lies about Somali Americans in Minnesota a central focus of his midterm campaign rallies, and the president’s inflammatory claims have been echoed by Minnesota Republicans.
House majority whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota, recently said on a conservative podcast: “I’ve got basically the Somali civil war that’s come to the state of Minnesota.”

The Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair-MN), community leaders, elected officials and ride-share driver groups were planning a press conference on Monday at the Hennepin County Medical Center to call for justice.

“Mohamed Yusuf should be home safe with his family, not fighting for his life after an attack fueled by hatred towards his Somali identity,” said Omar Fateh, a state senator in Minnesota, in a statement on social media. “We need answers and an immediate and transparent investigation.”

SEIU Local 26, a local labor union that organizes rideshare drivers, said in a social media post on the alleged attack: “We are shocked, angered and saddened by the news of the alleged attack that happened this weekend on Mohamed, a Minnesotan and Uber driver.”

A GoFundMe created on behalf of Yusuf and his family has already raised over $140,000. “As a result of this senseless assault, he suffered severe injuries and is now in a coma, fighting for his life,” the family wrote in the appeal for financial support.
“We are shocked and horrified by the details of this senseless attack,” a spokesperson for Uber said in an email.
“We banned the rider from the Uber platform, and we are keeping the driver and his loved ones in our thoughts. We stand ready to assist law enforcement with their investigation.”

articles.title: Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?
articles.summary: On the sidelines of the APEC summit this coming week, Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi Jinping, in the hopes of deepening economic and trade ties.

blocks.text: Politics·New

On the sidelines of the APEC summit this coming week, Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi Jinping, in hopes of deepening economic and trade ties.
It's the second meeting between the two leaders in less than a year, and this time it will take place in Shenzen, China, where the summit is being held on Wednesday and Thursday.
While Carney has been working to rebuild Canada's economic and trade relationship with China, experts warn that it doesn't mean the threat to Canada has weakened.

Canada's relationship with China might have improved, but the "serious national and economic security threats to Canada ... have not fundamentally changed," said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank with offices in Vancouver and Ottawa.

"What has changed is not China's behaviour but Canada's strategic circumstances and the Carney government's approach," she told CBC News. "With growing uncertainty in our relationship with the United States, there are compelling reasons to stabilize relations with Beijing, pursue economic opportunities and diversify our trade."

In an interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday, Jody Thomas, national security adviser to Justin Trudeau when he was prime minister, echoed Nadjibulla's views, adding that "the prime minister is pursuing an economic relationship, I hope, and I think with the understanding of the national security threat posed by China."

Speaking to reporters in Montreal on Tuesday, Carney said he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada, adding, "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly."

items: Carney embarks on a worldwide summit tour to build bridges with Europe and Asia

blocks.text: Carney said he would be bringing up the importance that Canada attaches "to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries."
The economic and trade relationship between Canada and China "is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we're involved," he said.
Nvidia spy scandal implications

It's hard to talk about national security threats from China without pointing to the much-publicized affair between Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday as CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia, and an alleged Chinese spy.

For Nvidia, the turmoil over the sex-and-spy scandal and Huang's resignation have cost in excess of $1 trillion US in market value. The political ramifications for U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration remain to be seen.

items: The Nvidia scandal has wiped away $1T in value. What that means for your investments
How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips

blocks.text: "What I hope doesn't get lost in all of this is the incredible vulnerability of this kind of concentration in our industry, in our economy and in our politics," former U.S. trade representative Katherine Tai told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"How vulnerable you become when you are so reliant on one company that makes one particular product that is apparently there to prop up the major growth industry in your economy. We here in the United States find ourselves in an incredibly precarious place."
Is the Nvidia scandal fracturing Trump's administration?
Carney shared a similar observation at Tuesday's news conference in Montreal.
Referring to China, Carney said, "In terms of the security risks of our partnership, they are much, much, much less than the security risks, for example, [faced by] the United States."
But Nadjibulla said the situation is a bit more nuanced than that.
Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank, is shown in Ottawa in June 2023. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
While the U.S. and China are "peer competitors" engaged in a global struggle for economic, technological and military leadership, Canada is in a fundamentally different position, she said.

"We are a much smaller, more open economy, with considerably less leverage in dealing with Beijing. That makes us more vulnerable to certain forms of economic coercion and political pressure, not less."

But even then, the question is not whether Canada faces the same level of risk as the U.S., Nadjibulla said. The question is whether Canada has the tools and capacity to manage the risks it does face.

items: Chinese authorities blocked Canada's Tiananmen Square tribute with trees, cherry picker: documents

blocks.text: Former national security adviser Jody Thomas points to Canada's own recent experience with alleged Chinese spying: the Canadian NATO intern who was arrested in July on charges of espionage allegedly tied to China.
Thomas said that incident and the Nvidia situation shed light on how China operates — but also how Canada needs to adapt to potential threats in the artificial intelligence space.

"What I think it means for Canada is that the approach the prime minister is taking with having a minister responsible for AI, setting up the [National Council on Artificial Intelligence], advising in terms of how to use that AI, how to regulate AI and how to ensure that the safety guardrails are developed."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Racy Rafique is a producer for CBC's national television program Power & Politics. She also works as a writer covering federal politics for CBC's parliamentary bureau from time to time. Racy was a 2023 CBC Joan Donaldson Scholar and is a graduate of Toronto Metropolitan University. You can reach her at racy.rafique@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Goodbye, overtourism? Sustainable travel gains ground
articles.summary: As tourism booms across Latin America, alternative forms of travel are gaining ground. Making your holiday more sustainable means rethinking who calls the shots, who invests and who benefits.

image.caption: Punta Cana, Dominican Republic — a tourism hot spot in Latin AmericaImage: Erika Santelices/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Latin America is currently one of the world's most dynamic tourism regions. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations agency responsible for promoting responsible tourism, international arrivals in South America grew by 7% last year, while Central America saw a 5% increase, both above the global average.

But the boom comes at a price: overtourism. In some destinations, the sheer number of visitors is creating environmental and social problems, fueling tensions and raising questions about who really benefits from the business.

One famous example is Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in Peru, which lures up to 5,600 visitors a day. In 2025, Peru's official watchdog warned that more tickets were being sold than permitted, potentially putting the site at risk of being added to UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. The UNESCO World Heritage Committee has already expressed its concern.

blocks.caption: People are flocking to Machu Picchu, the Inca citadel in PeruImage: Michalakis Ppalis/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a bid to protect the Galapagos Islands and its bountiful ecosystems that inspired Charles Darwin, Ecuador doubled the entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024. Even so, pressure is mounting to construct new hotels and tourist apartments. And in Mexico City, the influx of tourists and digital nomads into neighborhoods such as Roma and Condesa has fueled protests over rising rents.

blocks.caption: The Galapagos Islands introduced an entrance fee for foreign visitors to $200 in 2024Image: Alie Skowronski/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What can be done to make tourism more inclusive and sustainable? That's one of the industry's biggest questions. At ITB Americas, an international travel trade fair in Guadalajara, Mexico, DW spoke with three experts.
Sustainable travel moving from niche to mainstream

Richard Bazan is a regional manager for the Americas at Planeterra, a nonprofit organization that promotes and supports community-based tourism. He said several trends are emerging: group sizes are shrinking and travelers are seeking more intimate experiences.
"Where groups of 20 used to travel together, now it's four or five," he told DW.

So-called "nature-positive" tourism is also gaining traction, with travel programs that help fund, for example, reforestation projects. Bazan said even all-inclusive resorts are realizing that they can no longer shut themselves off from their surroundings. Instead, they need to offer authentic experiences that connect visitors with the destination.
"Community-based tourism is no longer a niche," he said.

blocks.caption: Mexico has been trying to contain a record surge of foul-smelling sargassum seaweed, fueled by a mix of nutrient-rich runoff and shifting ocean conditionsImage: Alfredo Estrella/AFP

blocks.text: Pressure for change is also coming from travelers themselves. According to Booking.com's 2025 annual survey, which polled 32,000 people in 34 countries, 93% said they wanted to make more sustainable travel choices. For the first time, more than half (53%) were aware of tourism's impact on local communities, not just the environment.
Communities know what's best for their land

Sarah Payne, director of the Reset Tourism Fund at the UnTours Foundation, pointed to the underlying problem. In the traditional tourism business model, most of the money generated never reaches local communities, the people who actually live with the influx of visitors.

"Access to financing is key, yet extremely difficult for communities," she explained. The financial products on the market tend to be expensive and inflexible, as tourism is considered a high-risk sector. Her foundation's fund offers low-interest loans with flexible repayment terms. Its guiding principle is that communities generally know what's best for their own land.

Sebastian Munoz, co-founder of Rutopia, a platform specializing in ecotourism and community-based tourism, has brought his experience from the nonprofit sector into social enterprise. His believes tours must be designed in partnership with communities so they feel a sense of ownership, rather than seeing them as something imposed from outside.
Saving Ladakh: Locals lead sustainable tourism drive

Bazan, meanwhile, thinks community-based tourism should not be approached as a humanitarian project, but through a market-driven lens: understanding what visitors are looking for and then planning hand-in-hand with the local community. In other words, building bridges between these two distinct worlds.
"It's not sustainable to create a product if no one comes to experience it," he said.
The challenge: Rethinking growth

The big question is how to grow without sacrificing sustainability. For Bazan, that decision doesn't belong to the tourism industry. Communities themselves must decide how they want to grow, and outside players should not pressure them. Their role, he said, is to amplify local voices, not to bring solutions or investments. "We have to learn to listen," he said.

The impact of community-based tourism is difficult to measure, Munoz acknowledged, because it has social impacts that go beyond the numbers. He cited the example of the Indigenous Mixtec community in Mexico that receives tourists interested in learning the local language. Suddenly, children who today speak only Spanish began joining the classes and asking their grandparents to teach them the language, too.

For Munoz, community-based tourism can be a powerful tool for valuing cultural and regional diversity. It's about creating value over the long term — and that, he said, is where the real experience for visitors lies.
The experts agree that change is slow. But they argue it's worth the effort: If there is more respect for local people and environments, in the end, everyone goes home happier.
This article was originally written in Spanish.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges removal of Starshield limits on Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine's government says the throttling of satellite-based internet system prevents Kyiv from intercepting Russian attacks.

image.caption: Zaporizhzhia was targeted overnight by russiaImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the US should remove any restrictions on the Starshield satellite internet system being removed.
Kyiv is "counting" on the move due to severe damage to civilian infrastructure as a result of Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said, also adding photos from eight locations in his country.
"The protection of lives and Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this," Zelenskyy posted on his X account.
The sattellite-based internet system was limited to slower speeds in October, with the limitations only being lifted due to Ukraine's criticism.

Ukraine leader Zelenskyy said he had instructed several ministries, including the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to "work as closely as possible" with the US and Starshield owner Elon Musk's SpaceX, also saying the system's throttling helped Russian attacks.

blocks.caption: A building was heavily damaged due to a Russian drone in Chornomorsk.Image: Nina Liashonok/REUTERS

blocks.text: According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine's interceptor drones are not effective due to losing connection with operators at the speed of 161 kilometers per hour. This results in the drones not being able to hit Russian drones or rockets.
Russian attacks continue

The past week, Russian attacks in Ukraine included more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 glide bombs and 15 missiles and cruise missiles, Zelenskyy said, calling Moscow's strikes "brutal" and saying they are "difficult to counter."
The US government and SpaceX gave in part contradictory answers to the question of who was responsible for the Starshield speed limit.
A Russian strike on the port city of Chornomorsk resulted in six injuries and damaged energy infrastructure, local authorities said.

blocks.caption: Zaporizhzhia was attacked several times in the past daysImage: Iwan Fedorow/Ratsverteidigung des Gebiets Saporischschja

blocks.text: According to the authorities, a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks was hit, thus leaving some 41,000 customers without power on a temporary basis.
Six people were also injured after Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with one of those injured being a two-year-old boy, according to Ukraine's emergency services.
Estonia said Russia was responsible for an attempted arson attack on a drone factory, with the border between the two countries to close, citing "clear evidence" Moscow is behind the attack.

articles.title: LSU star MiLaysia Fulwiley arrested after allegedly striking police officer with car
articles.summary:
• Guard allegedly tried to flee traffic stop in Baton Rouge

  • Tigers say they are aware of situation involving player

LSU guard MiLaysia Fulwiley, one of the…

blocks.text: LSU guard MiLaysia Fulwiley, one of the ninth-ranked Tigers’ leading scorers, was arrested after allegedly striking a police officer while attempting to flee from a traffic stop.

LSU’s athletic department, in a written statement provided to The Associated Press, said university officials “are aware of the situation and have no further comment at this time as it’s an ongoing legal matter.”
The arrest, first reported by WBRZ TV in Baton Rouge, occurred Saturday night as LSU’s football game against Texas was ending in the sold-out, 102,000-seat Tiger Stadium.

Authorities allege that an officer tried to stop the 21-year-old Fulwiley after observing her weaving through traffic, and that she drove away from the scene, the right front side of her vehicle striking a police officer. She allegedly sought to cut through a store parking lot before her vehicle was blocked by responding police.
Fulwiley was booked into East Baton Rouge Parish Prison on charges including aggravated battery, flight from an officer, aggravated assault and resisting an officer.
Fulwiley, who is averaging 17.8 points per game this season, scored a season-high 23 points during No 9 LSU’s 101-37 victory over Denver on Friday.
LSU are scheduled to play next at home on Monday night against Troy and Fulwiley’s availability for that game was unclear as of Sunday afternoon.

articles.title: ‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser
articles.summary:
Professor calls on ministers to use awareness triggered by Russell Brand conviction to examine use of rape myths in trials

The debate triggered by high profile cases must “pull back the…

blocks.text: The debate triggered by high profile cases must “pull back the curtain” on the treatment of people making allegations of sexual offences in the criminal justice system in England and Wales, the government’s independent adviser on rape has told the Guardian.

Prof Katrin Hohl, who has advised the government in an overhaul of how rape is treated by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said the government should use the public awareness triggered by Russell Brand’s conviction for rape to examine the use of rape myths and jury direction in trials.

“So many things are going wrong in our justice system when it comes to the treatment of victims of rape and sexual assault, but most of the time no one ever finds out what has happened during the investigation process or during a trial,” she said.

Hohl said that despite “significant progress” made by police forces and the CPS – who have been directed to make investigations more focused on suspects rather than victim behaviour under a system known as Operation Soteria – the court system was being left behind.

A report published by Hohl last month suggested sexual assault cases prepared under the new system were experiencing “a cliff edge” when they came to trial, and were potentially coming up against practices such as the use of rape myths by defence barristers.

“We essentially know very little about how rape and sexual assault cases play out in England and Wales and it is time to pull back the curtain,” said Hohl. “We need proper research into the actions of barristers, judges and juries during trials so that victims can actually get the justice the law says they should achieve.”

Hohl’s remarks come after the victims commissioner, Claire Waxman, called for a new legal duty on judges to direct juries, if rape myths have been ventured during a trial, stating: “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

During the Brand trial, which saw the comedian sentenced to more than 10 years in prison after he was found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, his barrister, Ian Winter, said Brand’s accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Government ministers are also understood to be considering calls for a “staggered” consent law, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds, after a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 launched a campaign for the law to be changed.

Mia Latter, who says she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16, told the Sunday Times: “I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

On Sunday, Pat McFadden said ministers would discuss the issue. Speaking to the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the work and pensions secretary said questions over a staggered age of consent have “been raised and will be discussed”, adding: “[I] can’t tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights.”
Since the trial, several support services for victims of sexual assault and rape said they had been experiencing a significant increase in the number of calls and messages to helplines.

Rape Crisis centres are experiencing “very significant demand” and phonelines have been inundated with calls since Brand was convicted of rape, said Ciara Bergman, chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales.
Many women are also now questioning their own experiences with older men, she said, after separate allegations were made public that David Walliams preyed on young women for sex.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sexual offence allegations against Walliams were being looked at by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News. One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”. Walliams denies any wrongdoing.
Bergman said calls to the 24/7 rape and sexual abuse support line had quadrupled since the start of the month, while rape crisis centres were reporting a massive rise in demand for help.

“That demand comes from a range of places,” she said. “There are people who see the news and are reminded of their own experiences and people who are retraumatised by seeing this issue in the news. But there are people who may have experienced predation and exploitation at vulnerable times in their lives, and they’re now beginning to question their own experiences.”

She echoed calls for greater transparency in trials, and argued the coverage of high profile cases had highlighted the gap in the public knowledge around the experience of going to trial and issues around consent.

“Our centres are adept at responding to victims but they are under very significant pressure,” she said. “When you look at these stories and the response to them there is no question about the need for more comprehensive support and more rape crisis centres so victims and survivors can get the justice they deserve.”
A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “We are always looking at ways we can improve how the justice system treats victims of sexual violence.

“That’s why we are changing the law to stop irrelevant evidence that relies on myths being weaponised against victims, rolling out specialist courtrooms for rape and serious sexual offences and improving support for victims, backed by our record £550m investment in support services.”

articles.title: Czechia: Scores protest against public media reform
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people attended the protest against the government's plan to abolish broadcasting fees. Critics say the nationalist coalition would like to secure control over the media.

image.caption: Protesters traveled from around Czechia to attend the protestImage: David W Cerny/REUTERS

blocks.text: A protest against plans to abolish broadcasting fees in Czechiadrew between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague, organizers said.
The amount of protesters resulted in overcrowded public transport, with many people traveling from other cities by bus and train.
According to protesters, the plan could bring public broadcasters under the control of the country's right-wing government under billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
Government denies takeover attempt
Babis himself defended the plan last week, saying that his government is not interested in controlling or nationalizing public media.

"None of what the people are protesting against… is true," he said. Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also replied to the criticism by accusing the protest's organizers of turning demonstrations into a business model.
Since its introduction in April, the plan resulted in several large-scale protests, with Czech TV and radio going on a one-day strike in protest against it.

blocks.caption: Hundreds of thousands of people attended the demonstration in PragueImage: David W Cerny/REUTERS

blocks.text: International groups have criticized the plan, including the European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists and Reporters Without Borders.

The government would like public broadcasters to be financed by the state budget rather than through fees, arguing that while the plan will not affect editorial independence, broadcasters need to cut costs. Critics accused the Czech government of wanting to secure more influence through the decision.
International criticism
The suggested media reform would result in public media's budget being cut down by 15 percent.
The current coalition in Czechia is made of Babis's ANO party, the far-right SPD and the Eurosceptic Motorists.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Andrej Babis rejected the protesters' criticismImage: Michaela Rihova/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: While the protests also saw the current coalition being criticized, polls show ANO still enjoys some 30 percent of support.

Per the Reuters Institute Digital News Report for 2026, trust in the media in Czechia is low and stands between 30 and 33 percent, with public broadcasters still being considered "the most trusted brands."

articles.title: Trident nuclear submarine concludes record underwater deployment
articles.summary:
HMS Vengeance’s seven-month patrol prompts concerns about slow pace of maintenance of ageing fleet and impact on crew

A Trident nuclear submarine has concluded a record seven-month…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: A Trident nuclear submarine has concluded a record seven-month deployment, returning to the Faslane naval base in Scotland where its crew was greeted by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting.

HMS Vengeance began its patrol on 12 April and spent 217 days submerged before returning on Sunday, having left the country when Keir Starmer was in Downing Street and Manchester United were third in the Premier League.

Its tour surpasses the previous 205-day record set by HMS Vanguard, and has raised questions about the strains placed on sailors and the reliability of ageing submarines sent on the extended missions.

“Patrols are getting longer and longer,” said David Cullen, a nuclear expert with the Basic thinktank. “The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world.”

The increase in the time spent at sea reflects the slow pace of submarine maintenance, prompting Labour to blame spending cuts implemented by the Conservatives, though naval chiefs insist there is a plan for improvement.
Streeting said the length of time the crew had spent submerged did not “sit lightly” with him.

Streeting, who was accompanied in Faslane by the first secretary of state, Lou Haigh, added: “It makes me feel even more indebted to the crew for the service they’ve given to the country, for the commitment they show, the dedication, the professionalism, the expertise.
“I think the whole country can be extraordinarily proud of our submariners and of our nuclear deterrent.”
He described the nuclear patrols as the “ultimate national endeavour” and thanked the returning submariners for their “dedicated, heroic service” which he said was the model of patriotism.

HMS Vengeance is one of four submarines that carryBritain’s Trident nuclear missiles. A boat is at sea at all times, so the UK could launch strikes even if land-based systems had been destroyed in a nuclear war.

When the Vanguard class of submarines was brought into service in the 1990s, they were designed to carry three to four months of food for the crew of about 140, and deployments of more than 100 days were considered highly exceptional. Missions now start with tinned food crammed into corridors and other available spaces.

Each submarine has to keep its location secret so it cannot be targeted, meaning it also cannot be resupplied. The boats maintain radio silence and so the crew cannot message out on the long deployments, though they can receive news and other information.

Such is the length of the patrols that the return of a Trident submarine, known as a “day zero”, has become a political event. Starmer made an unannounced visit when the last patrol ended in April, praising the crew on their return.

There have been worries about the psychological impact of the patrols on the crew members, who have to spend seven months underwater in a boat 150 metres long, at a time when the Royal Navy is struggling to recruit new personnel.

Last week, the head of the Royal Navy, Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for the Trident sailors, but added that the UK needed to “improve our submarine maintenance” to allow faster turnaround.

The submarine service, in line with the rest of the navy, has a “no touching rule” – prohibiting physical intimacy on board – though the service has had to contend with allegations of sexual abuse and harassment during deployments.

In October 2024, the then first sea lord was forced to issue an apology to women – who make up about 10% of the navy – who had suffered “misogyny, bullying and other unacceptable behaviours” in the submarine service.

The navy conducted an inquiry after a whistleblower, Sophie Brook, complained of a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” from male sailors. Reports of rape, physical and verbal abuse were examined in a heavily redacted report.

Trident submarines can carry 40 nuclear warheads, with enough destructive power to destroy Moscow and several other major Russian cities, and a letter from the prime minister to tell the captain how to proceed in the event it is determined the UK no longer exists after an all-out nuclear attack.

Such is the length of the boat’s patrol it will still be carrying Starmer’s letter, though the replacement submarine on rotation will have Andy Burnham’s instructions, written in longhand in the days after he took over at Downing Street.

In July, Labour announced a £26bn, 10-year plan to invest in Britain’s three main naval bases, at Faslane, the operational home of the Trident submarines, Devonport and Portsmouth, as part of a wider increase in defence spending.

However, the first of the replacements for the four Vanguard class submarines, HMS Dreadnought, is not expected to be ready until about 2032, meaning that the old boats have at least five more years to remain in service.
“The inherent risks of operating submarines are being pushed by them being run as they are. At the end of the submarines’ design life they should be run gently, not as hard as they are,” Cullen said.

articles.title: Satellite limitations imposed by Musk's SpaceX pose danger for Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that limitations on the Starshield satellite system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defences around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of…

image.caption: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks to the media at an airport in Dublin on Thursday. (Peter Morrison/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that limitations on the Starshield satellite system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defences around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.
Ukraine president warns restrictions hinder ability to stop Russian attacks on energy
Restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield satellite communications system are hindering its ability to intercept Russian drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He warned that limitations on the system, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, could weaken defenses around Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of the winter months, when Moscow has repeatedly targeted the power grid.

Ukraine's interceptor drones continue to lose contact with their operators when flying faster than 161 km/h along the front line and over Russian-occupied territory, leaving them unable to catch Russian Shahed drones, Zelenskyy said.

"We are counting on these restrictions to be lifted," he wrote on social media. "The protection of lives and Ukrainian energy infrastructure before winter depends on this. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the President's Office have been instructed to work closely with the American side and SpaceX.
"It is important to be on the right side of history. We need to help Ukraine."

Zelenskyy questioned Saturday whether the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite earlier assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under U.S. government control.
Outages after Russian strike on power facility
Meanwhile, a Russian strike on Chornomorsk, a port city in Ukraine's Odesa region, injured six people and damaged energy infrastructure, regional head Oleh Kiper said Sunday on Telegram.
The blast and falling debris also damaged a gas pipeline and nearby residential buildings, while two parked cars caught fire.

items: European security plan floated by U.S. would benefit Putin, Zelenskyy says

blocks.text: The strike hit a facility operated by DTEK Odesa Electric Networks, temporarily leaving about 41,000 customers without power, Kiper said.
A woman walks at the site of a building damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the city of Chornomorsk, Odesa region, on Nov. 15, 2026. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)
Overnight Russian airstrikes on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia injured another six people, including a two-year-old boy, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Sunday.
Russia launched more than 2,300 drones, 1,590 guided aerial bombs and 15 missiles of various types against Ukraine over the past week, Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian attack kills 1 in Russia's Rostov
Ukrainian drone strikes damaged two electrical substations in Russia's Rostov region, killing a chief engineer, Gov. Yuri Slyusar said Sunday.

Four people were injured when drone debris fell on their cars, Slyusar wrote on social media. A fifth person was wounded when debris struck a "production facility" in the village of Troitskoye, he said.

Ukrainian forces also targeted Russia's Tatarstan region, officials said. Radmir Belyaev, mayor of Nizhnekamsk, the region's third-largest city, said a "large-scale and prolonged attack" damaged its industrial zone.
Six people were injured, and heating and hot water supplies were disrupted in parts of the city, he said.

Ukraine's General Staff said it had hit two sites in Nizhnekamsk: Nizhnekamskneftekhim, one of the largest petrochemical complexes in Europe, and a production site operated by petrochemical company Sibur. An oil refinery in the area was also hit, it said.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces shot down 533 Ukrainian drones overnight across 13 Russian regions, the Russian-annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
Drones damage Black Sea ships, Romania says

Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said Sunday that three commercial vessels in the Black Sea were struck by drones overnight, the latest in a string of attacks that have raised fears of the war spilling over into NATO territory.
"Once again, maritime security in the Black Sea has been threatened," Niculescu wrote on X.

Romania's Ministry of National Defense said a Greek-flagged oil tanker was struck by a drone, sparking a fire that was extinguished by the crew. Two more ships were later struck by drones, and their crews also extinguished fires onboard, the ministry said. No casualties were reported and the ministry did not state the origin of the drones.

items: Black Sea sailors thought a rescue boat was racing toward them. Instead, it was a drone that sank their ship

blocks.text: "These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law," Niculescu said, adding that they "reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine."
A rescuer works at the site of an apartment buildings damaged by a Russian air strike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Reuters)

Last month, a string of cargo ships and tankers were struck by aerial or naval drones near the Bulgarian and Romanian coastlines. At least 30 sailors on commercial ships were confirmed dead or reported missing.

"We will continue to take all necessary measures, alongside our Allies, to strengthen security in the Black Sea," Niculescu added. "This remains a key priority for the Government, in close co-operation with our regional partners and NATO."
Estonia threatens Russian border closure

Estonia's government said Sunday it would close all border crossings with Russia from Dec. 1, after the Baltic country's prime minister accused Moscow of attempting to sabotage an Estonian drone company a day earlier.

The government said an attempted attack had been carried out early Saturday against Threod Systems in Viimsi, north of the capital, Tallinn, "with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire."

"If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face," Prime Minister Kristen Michal said in a statement.
"Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia's defense industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable," Michal added.
National broadcaster ERR reported Sunday that eight Latvian nationals have been detained after the attempted break-in.

articles.title: Russia will not compete at world junior hockey championship in Alberta, IIHF says
articles.summary: The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed that Russia will not compete at the 2027 world junior hockey championship in Alberta due to restrictions imposed by the Canadian government.

image.caption: The IIHF logo is seen on the jersey of Canadian player at IIHF World Junior Hockey Championship semifinals game against Czechia, on Jan. 4 in St. Paul, Minn. (Matt Krohn/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Hockey·Breaking
The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed that Russia will not compete at the 2027 world junior hockey championship in Alberta due to restrictions imposed by the Canadian government.
2027 World Juniors will take place in Edmonton, Red Deer from Dec. 26 - Jan. 5
The International Ice Hockey Federation confirms in a statement that Russia will not have a team at the world junior hockey championship next month in Alberta.

The IIHF says Russia will not be able to play at the tournament starting Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer, despite a mandate for the country's reinstatement from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, due to restrictions put in place by the federal government.
The organization says Canada will remain as host despite going against the CAS's ruling.
Russia and Belarus have been banned from competing in international hockey tournaments since 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
The CAS mandated Russia's reinstatement in an Oct. 30 ruling, but days later Prime Minister Mark Carney said Russians and Belarusians would be barred from competing regardless of that decision.

The impasse left the tournament in limbo, with Norway's federation saying it would be bumped from the competition in favour of a Russian team, while hockey officials from Russia suggested the tournament should be moved elsewhere.
The CAS's decision was met with immediate pushback, with hockey federations from Sweden, Finland, Czechia and other nations refusing to play against a reinstated Russian team.

articles.title: Estonia closes border to Russia after suspected drone factory arson
articles.summary: Estonia has accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare after a drone factory was set alight in Viimsi. Now it will close its border crossings at the start of December.

image.caption: Estonia was one of the few EU states that allowed border crossings to and from RussiaImage: Hendrik Osula/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Estonia foiled an attempted Russian arson attack on a drone fractory, authorities said on Sunday, prompting the country to close all border crossings with its larger neighbor.
Prime Minister Karsten Michal said that Russia's GRU intelligence service had attempted to sabotage the Estonian defence company Threod Systems in Viimsi on Saturday night.
He said "extensive damage" had been averted after a response by law enforcement, who detained the suspected attackers.
"This is part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," Michal said.
There was no immediate comment from Russia.
Estonia to close border crossings with Russia
Hours after the announcement, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the country would close all border crossings with Russia by December 1.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered," he said on social media.
"Closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia and strengthen our efforts to prevent sanctions circumvention."
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare
Tsahkna said he informed his Finnish, Latvian, and Lithuanian counterparts of the decision.
Estonia has a number of border crossings with Russia, and has until now remained one of the few European Union member states that allowed crossings.

articles.title: Nearly 1,600 migrants arrive on Spain's Canary Islands in one day
articles.summary: The majority of the migrants who arrived on the islands on Saturday came from Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. The surge in arrivals to the Canaries comes after Spain's Ceuta recently faced a migration…

image.caption: Most boats departing for the Canary Islands come from Mauritania (FILE: November 12, 2026)Image: Borja Suarez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nearly 1,600 migrants arrived on the Spain's Canary Islands in one day, Spanish news agency EFE reported Sunday, using tallies from the Spanish government's Maritime Safety and Rescue Society.
What do we know so far about the migrant arrivals on the Canaries?
Most of the 1,580 migrants who came ashore on Saturday landed on the island of El Hierro. They arrived aboard 15 wooden fishing boats.

Most of the migrants came from West African countries such as Senegal, Gambia, and Guinea. Between Friday and Saturday, over 2,300 migrants in total arrived on the islands, according to the Spanish authorities.
The Canary Islands, whose shortest gap with Africa is around 100 kilometers (around 62 miles), faces a migration crisis.

Spanish Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres Perez visited the town of La Restinga on Sunday, which lies on the southernmost tip of El Hierro. She met with residents of the town and thanked them for "their solidarity and commitment" as the island witnesses a large number of migrant arrivals.

blocks.caption: The Red Cross is providing medical help and assistance to the migrants arriving in El Hierro (FILE: November 11, 2026)Image: Borja Suarez/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The Government of Spain continues to work to ensure that this surge in migration is managed with humanity and with the island's residents in mind," she posted on X. El Hierro has a population of nearly 12,000 people.

Although the Canary Islands a large number of migrants arriving on its shores over the weekend, overall migration to the islands is down 5.5% between January and October 31 from the same period last year.
Canary Island arrivals surge come after recent Ceuta crisis
The surge in latest arrivals to the Canary Islands comes after another Spanish territory, Ceuta, faced a migration crisis in late July.
Meet the woman feeding 100s of Ceuta's migrants

An estimated 80,000 people, mostly young Moroccan men, crossed into Ceuta from neighboring Morocco. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, a member of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE), has faced criticism from the opposition over his handling of the crisis.
Migration, along with housing, are expected to be major topics for voters as they head for snap elections in Spain later this month.

articles.title: Estonia to close all border crossings with Russia after attack on drone maker
articles.summary:
Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack Estonian PM links to Tallinn’s support for Ukraine

Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a…

blocks.text: Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.

On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.

Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.

blocks.caption: Kristen Michal announced the border closure to ‘send a clear message that attacks are unacceptable’. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.

He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine. “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine,” Michal said.

blocks.caption: Margus Tsahkna said: ‘Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences.’ Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying: “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”
Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.
It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that authorities have attributed to Russia, following an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.

In September, Kapo said it was confident that incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”. The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.

At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.

Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks against defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries on messaging platforms online to carry out acts of sabotage.

Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.

articles.title: Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions and be on 'right side of history'
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says restrictions are still in place and making it difficult to stop Russian attacks.

blocks.text: Ukraine uses the normal Starlink service for communications on the battlefield, while Starshield is used for the interception of missiles and drones in Ukraine airspace.
The issue of speed restrictions was first identified in October. It led to conflicting accounts by both Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump.
Musk said the US government was responsible as Starshield was controlled by them, but Trump denied being responsible and said he had told the billionaire owner to "put it back".
It appeared to be returning to normal after a week, following which Ukraine said the restrictions were still being implemented.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic stand-off between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, had pushed global prices higher.

On Sunday Zelensky said Ukraine was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones targeting electricity substations because "restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there".

"Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161km/h (100mph) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered 'shaheds'," he posted, referring to the drones that follow an Iranian design.
Ukraine has also been beset by a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors used to defend against Russian missiles - a situation that Russia has exploited to intensify strikes on Ukrainian targets.
Overnight and into Sunday morning Russia hit energy infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and the Sumy, Odesa, Zhytomyr, and Kirovohrad regions, Ukraine said.
It also struck railway infrastructure in the Dnipro, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
Scores of people are said to have been hurt in those attacks, as well as two in the Donetsk and Kyiv regions.
Two people were killed in an attack on an infrastructure facility in Chernihiv Region's Mena, governor Vyacheslav Chaus said.
Multiple strikes were also delivered on energy facilities across the region, he added on Telegram.
Ukraine meanwhile said it had carried out strikes on a petrochemical plant and an oil refinery in the central Russian city of Nizhnekamsk.
"On the night of November 15, units of Ukraine's Defence Forces reached Nizhnekamsk in Tatarstan," the military said on Telegram.
"Two enterprises that feed the Russian war with raw materials and fuel came under attack."
Other Ukrainian strikes killed one person in Taganrog, an industrial port city near the border, regional governor Yuri Slyusar said.
In the occupied Luhansk region a lorry driver and an elderly woman were also killed, Leonid Pasechnik, the regional leader installed by Moscow said.
Meanwhile Estonia has announced it will shut its border crossing points with Russia from 1 December following a suspected sabotage attack on a defence company.
Eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Estonian authorities say they had been ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence service to try and carry out the attack. Russia has not commented.
"Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
