articles.title: Brazilian President Lula invites Marcos to visit Brazil
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva invited President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to visit Brazil next year, as the two countries recently held bilateral talks in Manila.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 5:12pm
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva invited President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to visit Brazil next year, as the two countries recently held bilateral talks in Manila.
Da Silva made the statement during a press briefing on Sunday as he concludes his two-day visit to the Philippines, according to GMA News Bea Pinlac's social media post.
He said Marcos was among the heads of state he invited to visit Brazil.
“We’re inviting everyone to come and visit Brazil,” Da Silva said, which was translated in English by a device provided by the Brazil delegation.
He added that Brazil aims to promote and collaborate with other countries in “exploration, transformation, industrialization,” among others.
Da Silva also hopes that Brazil will be a "definitive partner of ASEAN."
Malacañang said it has yet to confirm Brazil's invitation through the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Da Silva's visit coincided with the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits being held from November 15 to 17 in Pasay City.
Brazil, meanwhile, is a sectoral dialogue partner of ASEAN.
The bilateral meeting between the Philippines and Brazil tackled ways to enhance relations between the two countries.
The talks of the two leaders covered cooperation in multilateral forums and among countries of the Global South, according to the Presidential Communications Office.
Lula’s state visit also marks the first time a sitting Brazilian president visited the Philippines.
It also coincides with the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries this year.—Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Canada is spending more than ever on health care. Are we getting our money's worth?

image.caption: Long wait times, difficulty finding family doctors and gaps in services have prompted health policy experts to question whether Canada's health-care system needs more fundamental changes to how care is delivered. (CBC News )

blocks.text: Canada is spending more on health care than ever. Whether Canadians are getting more care for their money is another question.

A new report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), an independent, non-profit organization that collects and analyzes data on Canada's health-care system, projects health-care spending will reach a record $433 billion in 2026, or $10,398 per person, an increase of 4.8 per cent over last year.
For the first time since the pandemic, inflation-adjusted spending per person is expected to surpass its previous peak, reached in 2021.

But Canada already ranks among the higher-spending countries in the developed world, while patients continue to struggle with long wait times, overcrowded hospitals and difficulty finding family doctors.
That raises a central question: Is Canada spending enough on health care, or does the problem lie in how that money is being spent?

"I believe that these records of spending are just buying us more of the same right now," said Jason Sutherland, a professor at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and director of the Centre for Health Services and Policy Research.
He argues that without substantial changes to how health care is organized and delivered, additional spending is unlikely to produce meaningful improvements for patients.
1 in 10 Canadians waiting more than 14 hours in emergency rooms: report
Is $10,000 per person a lot?

The $10,398 figure represents the combined cost of publicly and privately funded health care, including hospitals, doctors, prescription drugs and services paid for through private insurance or directly by patients. It is not the amount each Canadian pays in taxes.
While the figure may seem substantial, international comparisons provide important context.
According to the CIHI report, Canada devoted 11.5 per cent of its gross domestic product to health care in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 9.3 per cent.
That placed Canada alongside other high-spending countries, including France at 11.3 per cent and Sweden at 11.2 per cent, but below Germany at 12.2 per cent and the United States at 17.2 per cent.
"We are not cheap in our health-care spending," Sutherland said.
LISTEN | Ontario doctors demand an apology over provincial letters urging reduced hours and delayed care:
Here and Now Toronto7:49Why is the Ontario Ministry of Health asking doctors to scale back their hours and delay patient care?

Sara Allin, an associate professor at the University of Toronto's Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, agreed that Canada's spending is substantial. But she said the more revealing comparison is what countries achieve with their investments.
She pointed to data showing Canada performs relatively well on some measures, including life expectancy and vaccination rates, but continues to lag in important areas of access and service delivery.
"We have very persistently long wait times," Allin said. "We have persistent challenges with care co-ordination."
She described Canada's health system as generally a middle performer among countries with similarly high expenditures.
His cancer drug costs $90,000/month. Doctors say it’s greed
More money, but where is it going?
The CIHI report identifies a potentially important change in how health-care spending is growing.
Inflation-adjusted spending per person is projected to grow 2.3 per cent this year, compared with just 0.4 per cent in 2025.
More significantly, CIHI estimates public-sector spending will increase by more than $5 billion beyond what is needed to keep pace with inflation and demographic changes.

Adam Rondeau, CIHI's manager of health spending and operations analytics, said the increase could be an early indication that governments are investing in additional capacity, new technologies and innovations in health-care delivery.
But determining precisely where that money is going is more complicated.

items: Your genes could change your prescription. So why aren't doctors testing?
Your questions about this year's federal budget, answered

blocks.text: "It's difficult to say X number of dollars is net new and related to a given program of work," Rondeau said.
He explained that the report identifies additional spending but cannot establish whether that investment is producing shorter wait times, more available services or better patient outcomes.
Meanwhile, the report states that spending on physicians is projected to increase 8.3 per cent this year, substantially faster than overall health-care spending.
Yet access to primary care remains a major challenge. CIHI's research on primary care found that 17 per cent of Canadian adults reported having no regular health-care provider in 2023.

Sara Allin, an associate professor of health policy at the University of Toronto, says Canada spends more on health care than many comparable countries, but it continues to struggle with long wait times and access to services. (Submitted by Sara Allin)
Spending more isn't necessarily spending better
For Allin, the challenge isn't simply increasing health-care budgets; it's ensuring that additional investment produces measurable improvements.
"If we're spending this much, it's more perhaps how we're spending it than the level of spending at this point in terms of driving further improvements," she said.
One important difference between Canada and some comparable countries, she said, is how health care is financed.
According to CIHI's expenditure figures, 71.4 per cent of Canada's health spending is projected to come from public sources in 2026, with the remaining 28.6 per cent financed privately.

Allin said several other wealthy countries fund a larger share of health care collectively, allowing them to cover a broader range of services, including prescription drugs, dental care and mental health supports.
She said those differences have consequences for both efficiency and equity.
Publicly financed systems can negotiate lower prices and reduce some administrative costs, she explained. They can also reduce financial barriers that prevent patients from accessing needed services.
Hundreds of unionized health-care workers rally outside legislature
Allin said gaps in Canada's public coverage mean people without adequate private insurance can face substantial costs for necessary services, particularly prescription drugs and mental health care.
She also questioned whether Canada's health-care financing arrangements provide sufficient incentives to improve patient outcomes.
Rather than simply paying providers according to the volume of services delivered, Allin said governments could do more to link funding with measurable improvements in care.
Sutherland similarly argued that governments need to rethink where additional resources are directed.

items: Canada's health ministers say federal funding extension only delays looming 'fiscal cliff'
Cost of Canadian Dental Care Plan exceeded budget by $1.1B in first 2 years: auditor general

blocks.text: He pointed to home care, assisted living, long-term care and other community-based services as areas where greater investment could help keep patients out of overcrowded hospitals and emergency departments.
Both experts also raised concerns about the pressure that rising health-care spending could place on other public priorities, including education, housing and social services.

Ultimately, Sutherland said, the figures should reassure Canadians that substantial resources are being devoted to health care while also prompting them to question whether those resources are being used effectively.

"I think they should be somewhat relieved that Canada is not underfunding this health-care system, but at the same time, they should be concerned that they're not getting great value for their money."

articles.title: Scientists race to discover and protect what lives in the ocean
articles.summary: Scientists say not knowing what lives in our oceans holds back efforts to protect them. Marine biologists are racing to catalogue species — from carnivorous sponges to otherworldly sea slugs. Here's…

image.caption: A crustacean called an isopod perches on a sea pen. It was photographed during an Ocean Census expedition in the South Sandwich Islands, northeast of the Antarctic Peninsula. (Paul Satchell/The Nippon Foundation-Nekton Ocean Census)

blocks.text: Scientists say not knowing what lives in our oceans is holding back efforts to protect them. Because of that, many are racing to discover and document the wild and diverse species in marine environments that are often hard for humans to access.

Ocean Census, a global collaboration of scientists and non-profit organizations, estimates that scientists have documented less than 10 per cent of some 2.2 million fish, marine mammals, shellfish, plankton, squid, jellyfish and other species that live in our oceans.
"It's very difficult to protect what you don't know," said Michelle Taylor, head of science at Ocean Census.

A sea cucumber with horned appendages, nicknamed Loki, and a bright red-orange coral with fans of slender branches are among 57 new species announced and identified in October from an Ocean Census expedition off Argentina last year.

This new sea cucumber species was nicknamed Loki because of its prominent horned appendages, reminiscent of the god in Norse mythology. It was found in the Mar del Plata submarine canyon off Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
A striking, bright red-orange octocoral was photographed nearly 2,000 metres below the surface of the ocean in Argentina's Mar del Plata canyon. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A landmark UN biodiversity agreement in 2022 committed to protecting 30 per cent of the world's land, water and marine areas by 2030, but has been falling short on ocean protection, with just 12 per cent of oceans (compared to 27 per cent of lands) set to be protected by 2030.
Canada has so far protected 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS).
Claire Goodwin, a research scientist at Huntsman Marine Science Centre in St. Andrew's, N.B., said the goal is to protect areas with high biodiversity.
"But if you're not surveying some of your marine life and you don't know what's living there, you can't say which those biodiverse areas are."
A cone jelly captured by the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian off the coast of Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
Sponges that eat meat, provide housing
The problem is that even within Canada, many areas are difficult to explore. Goodwin was part of an expedition in the Saguenay Fjord in Quebec in 2023.
On its steep walls, where only one species of sponge had previously been recorded, her team discovered 20 or 30 sponge species, including some new to science.
Carnivorous sponges were found in Quebec's Saguenay Fjord in 2023. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Among them were carnivorous sponges that trap shrimp with glass, velcro-like appendages to engulf and digest slowly, "which was really exciting," said Goodwin, since most sponges are passive filter feeders.

Goodwin says sponges have important roles in the ecosystems — as food for sea stars, homes for some worms and a place to lay eggs for some fish. Sponges in Canadian waters can also grow to half the size of an adult human.
Claire Goodwin collects sponges in the Bay of Fundy off the coast of New Brunswick. (Torben Brydges/Fisheries and Oceans Canada)

The sea slug Dendronotus yrjargul was recorded on a recent expedition led by the Innu Nation. It was the first time the species has been found off the coast of Canada. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC/Innu Nation)

Now Goodwin is working with the Innu Nation in Labrador to survey uncharted waters in their territory. "We literally don't know what the seabed's going to be like, let alone what's going to be living on it."
Climate change impacts and solutions
The race is on to find out as the ocean warms rapidly, and climate change shifts where species are found.

Already, Goodwin says, some species have completely disappeared from regions where they were once common. She points to basket stars, "really cool sea stars that have branching arms," which were once common around St. Andrew's, but haven't been seen there since a rapid warming around 2016.
A basket star, Gorgonocephalus arcticus, is seen in the Saguenay Fjord. The species used to be common in the Bay of Fundy but seems to have disappeared due to climate change. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)
Loïc Jacquemot, a postdoctoral researcher at Université du Québec à Rimouski, said in many areas, we don't even have much of a baseline from which to compare changes.

He's currently surveying Baffin Bay off the coast of Nunavut using a technique called eDNA, which identifies species from DNA shed into the water by organisms' skin, poop and tissues. That way, they can be surveyed without actually seeing or catching them — all you need is a water sample.
Loïc Jacquemot samples water for eDNA in B.C.'s coastal fjords. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)
He said species adapted to colder waters are expected to move into a smaller and smaller area "because, of course, they cannot go much more north," while warmer water species may expand their range.

That can have big impacts on things like the food chain — including fish and shellfish humans eat — and on the way carbon is moved around the ocean by zooplankton species that migrate each day between the depths and the surface.
"It's important for the climate because all these changes impact the way carbon is stored in the ocean," Jacquemot said.

This tiny copepod is one of 20 new species identified by the Ocean Census in October. These organisms are among the zooplankton that move carbon between the surface and depths of the ocean. (The Nippon Foundation-Nekton Ocean Census/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
Photosynthetic algae called diatoms from fjords in Greenland. Diatoms are important for capturing carbon dioxide in the oceans. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

The carbon stored by the ocean and its species is known as blue carbon. So far it includes 30 per cent of carbon dioxide generated by humans, along with 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by climate change, said a recent UN report, which warned that the ocean's ability to absorb more CO2 and heat is weakening.
Meanwhile, coral reefs, known as biodiversity hotspots with the ability to store huge amounts of carbon, are one of the ecosystems most threatened by climate change.

The impact of the ocean and its species on climate change are at the forefront of this year's UN climate summit, COP31, underway in Antalya, Turkey. Protecting marine ecosystems and "unlocking blue carbon for climate resilience" is one of 10 items on the meeting's "action agenda."

This week at COP31, former U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and groups representing island states pushed for a strong reference to oceans in next year's global "stocktake" of climate policies, supported by the European Union and African countries.
This grenadier fish was observed with parasitic copepods attached to its head during a 2025 Ocean Census expedition off Montagu Island near Antarctica. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)
This marine worm, Harmothoe imbricata, was found off Canada's Atlantic coast. (Christy Carr/HMSC)
For the 'biogeochemical functioning of our planet'

Taylor with Ocean Census said marine ecosystems are important for humans — even people who live far from the sea, not just for producing food and medicines, but also on a bigger scale. "You know, it's part of the biogeochemical functioning of our planet. We're very reliant on it, whether we realize it or not."
Taylor, Goodwin and Jacquemot all hope that by sharing with people the amazing diversity of life in the ocean, they can help people appreciate the importance of saving it.
"When we show people pictures and videos of what's underwater, they're always amazed by what we actually have down there," Goodwin said.
Michelle Taylor, head of science for Ocean Census, checks out views from the cameras on the ROV SuBastian during a mission to catalogue deep sea species. (Paul Satchell)
Taylor describes them as an incredible diversity of "wild looking creatures" and says for some of them "you wouldn't believe they were of this planet."

She said she's very worried about coral reefs especially, but "you have to have the attitude that there are solutions to this." In the meantime, she added, "we need to find as many species as we can, so we can understand diversity on this planet before it is lost."

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

articles.title: Why researchers are using drones to keep polar bears and people apart
articles.summary: While studies have shown drone hazing to be effective on black bears, researchers are now trying to see if it works with polar bears — a bigger, more curious and more aggressive species. The goal is…

image.caption: Kyle Garrett flies a drone near Churchill, Man., where he's testing whether he can use the device to scare polar bears out of areas where they might come into conflict with people. (Polar Bears International)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

While studies have shown drone hazing to be effective on black bears, researchers are now trying to see if it works with polar bears — a bigger, more curious and more aggressive species. The goal is to adapt the technology to Canada's North and try to take some of the risk out of managing the bears.
In Churchill, Man., climate change makes bear management a pressing issue
Researcher Kyle Garrett is looking at the viewfinder as his drone takes off, making a loud whirring sound as it zips low over the subarctic tundra in Churchill, Man.
Soon, he spies a lone adult polar bear, which looks right at the drone's camera.
"We want to see, does it scare them?" said Garrett. "Does it steer them into places we want them to go?"
For a split second, the bear ducks its head and broadens its stance defensively, as it assesses a foreign object it's likely never encountered before.

Garrett, a master's student from Utah's Brigham Young University, is experimenting with aerial drone hazing, an emerging wildlife management technique currently being used by the U.S. Department of Agriculture and Federal Aviation Administration.
An adult polar bear stares up at the camera of a drone. (Polar Bears International)

While studies have shown drone hazing to be effective on black bears, Garrett is trying to see if it works with polar bears — a bigger, more curious and more aggressive species. The goal is to adapt the technology to Canada's North and try to take some of the risk out of managing the bears.
Why bear deterrence is a pressing concern
Around Churchill, polar bear deterrence is a serious issue requiring serious balance.
The town, which is located on the southwestern shore of Hudson Bay, roughly 1,000 kilometres north of Winnipeg, is the self-proclaimed polar bear capital of the world.

It sits in the middle of the migration path for one of the largest populations of the largest land predator on earth. And every fall, thousands of people come to watch the bears gather on the shores of Hudson Bay to wait for it to freeze.
LISTEN | How bear hazing went high-tech:
Quirks and Quarks9:08Bear hazing goes high-tech with drones
The bears spend their winters hunting on the sea ice, though the warming climate has meant the bay ices over less predictably and later in the fall.
"The longer the bears are off the ice the more likely the bears are to come where people are," said Doug Clark, an expert on polar bear-human conflicts at the University of Saskatchewan.
"These aren't just skinny desperate bears, it's all bears, they all will come around [and] that creates situations that you certainly need to be on guard in."
The polar bear experiment
This fall Garrett is running the experiment in Churchill along with a couple of communities in northern Ontario and Nunavut.
In his drone video from the field, the bear begins to look curious as Garrett flies closer and directly over it, turning and braking the drone to make more loud whirring sounds.
The drone is far enough away to not touch the bear, but close enough to make it uncomfortable, and soon the bear starts to walk in the direction that Garrett is trying to nudge it.
"Once it kind of realizes, 'hey, I don't really like that,' then they move on their way," said Garrett.

items: 'It's their area too': How people in Churchill have learned to live with polar bears
Churchill adapts and thrives as warming climate threatens polar bear tourism

blocks.text: One day, he says, it might be possible for a conservation officer to deter a bear from coming too close to humans from the safety of their office.
"We're mainly thinking about the distance we can be from the animal while hazing it out of areas."
Polar bears have been known to approach and attack people. This time of year, residents leave doors unlocked in case someone needs to get away from a bear quickly.
As ice floes shrink, more polar bears are encountering humans
The Manitoba government tracks "bear occurrences" in Churchill. An occurrence can range from simply a bear sighting to an actual confrontation.

According to the province's latest report, this bear season there have been nearly 300 occurrences. Fifteen of those have resulted in bears being captured by conservation officials, either to be relocated or held in Churchill's special "polar bear jail," a facility in an old military hanger where problem bears can be held until the ice forms.
Watch a polar bear air lift from Churchill's 'bear jail'
The town runs a Polar Bear Alert program, which has long relied on the public and conservation officers to call in bear sightings. Now, PBI is looking to technology.

In addition to drones for deterrence and surveillance, it is also experimenting with what it calls Bear-dar, a radar system focused on detecting bears nearing town along with a network of mobile surveillance cameras it's calling Bear-vision.
"We want to bring additional eyes to the table," said Geoffrey York, vice president of science and policy for PBI.
"This would allow conservation officers to have a fairly low cost system that could be portable, something they could deploy in the field that would give them eyes on kind of problem spots."
A 'Bear-dar' system is installed near Churchill. (Elbert Bakker/Polar Bears International)
Questions the research still has to answer
As for the drone, Garrett says there is still a lot to learn about its limitations in Canada's rugged north, including how reliable the equipment is in the cold.
But the biggest questions are about the bears themselves — how they react and possibly adapt. It's possible that something that works now may lose its effectiveness over time.
"If a certain bear is droned often or daily it very well could become habituated to it," said Garrett.
But he says early results are promising.
"Be safe, and keep the bears wild. That's what we're hoping for."

items: Woman recounts harrowing attack by Churchill polar bear
Paddler shoots and kills polar bear along Hudson Bay coast in Manitoba, says province

blocks.text: ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Cameron MacIntosh is a senior reporter with CBC national news based in Winnipeg. He has spent most of his career in Western Canada while covering stories across the country and abroad for CBC News.

articles.title: English was the language I built my career in. In Canada, it became something to prove
articles.summary: Anusuya Datta had never given a second thought to knowing English, having always written and spoken in the language. After moving to Saskatchewan, people continually remarked on her English skills,…

image.caption: Anusuya Datta, seen here speaking at an international scientific conference, has had more than a decade of experience breaking down science concepts into plain-spoken English. But as an immigrant arriving in Saskatchewan, she found her skills in English were seen as an accomplishment in and of thems

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·First Person

Anusuya Datta had never given a second thought to knowing English, having always written and spoken in the language. After moving to Saskatchewan, people continually remarked on her English skills, both in complimentary and derogatory ways.
After moving to Canada, people kept reminding me English was my second language
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Nov 15, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
This First Person column is written by Anusuya Datta, a writer and journalist based in Saskatoon. For more information about First Person stories, see the FAQ.
I had only been in Canada for two weeks when I got the question that would follow me around for the next few years.
I’d gone to the pharmacy to ask about medication. The woman behind the counter looked up and said, “You speak very good English.”
By then, I had spent more than 15 years earning my living in English. Now I was being congratulated for successfully asking about a prescription.
“Thank you,” I said.
“Where did you learn it?”
“In India.”
She looked impressed.
I walked out with my prescription and a piece of information: in Canada, my English was an accomplishment.
Anusuya Datta attends a space conference, posing with a therapeutic robot seal proposed as a companion for astronauts on long missions. (Submitted by Anusuya Datta)

I had assumed I was the one immigrating. It turned out there were two of us. My English had done its paperwork. Canada makes you declare your English. That's what the international English language test is for. My English did very well. We both assumed that was the end of it. But someone had forgotten to send Saskatchewan a copy.

English wasn't the first language I learned, I admit. But it was the one I was educated in. I read novels in it and did a master's in it. Nobody in India ever congratulated me on it. It was like having elbows. You don't get complimented on elbows.
Coming face-to-face with assumptions

The pharmacist wasn’t the last. Neighbours told me I spoke English well. Doctors told me. People in shops told me, with the warmth usually reserved for someone who has parallel parked a combine. They were being kind to a newcomer, and I was grateful. I still am.
I said thank you. Every time. You don't hold up the queue to explain English isn't rocket science, and that you have, in fact, explained rocket science in it.
I have an accent when I speak English
Then my English got a job. So did I, at the same tech company in Saskatoon, which was convenient. We were both hired at a junior level. That seemed fair. We were new.

Soon my English was fine-tuning everyone's copy. Colleagues sent me their drafts the way you send a shirt to the dry cleaner, without conversation and expecting it back clean. My English had become the office Wi-Fi. Everyone used it. You don’t promote the Wi-Fi.
Eventually, I brought up a promotion on a call with my boss. I was told it was too soon. I didn't have the necessary experience.
“You need to be patient. These things take time,” he repeated, a little too slowly, as if he were weighing my English comprehension skills.
After the call, I sat for a long time. What my English lacked, I understood, was Canadian experience. It had only the other kind, where you do the work.
A year later, I joined an agriculture-technology company. I imagined data and software. The company sold agricultural chemicals in jugs.

This isn’t an attack on chemicals. Chemicals have had a long and successful career in agriculture. Jugs, for their part, have performed admirably throughout human civilization. But I couldn’t understand how the company involved technology.

The company wanted lots of content, the kind that sounds like the future of food. So I asked what the technology was. In my line of work, this is a standard opening question. It turned out to be a hostile act.
I was given a few words. Innovation. Sustainability. Transformation. None was attached to anything. My job was to expand them. I asked for details. I was told to read up.

So I read everything I could find and came back with questions. The boss came back with more keywords. Then the words started changing their meaning. One week, sustainability was the next big thing. The next, it was “woke.”

Finally, I asked why he was saying the exact opposite of what he’d said the week before. That was when he explained the problem. I wasn't understanding his feedback because English wasn't my first language.

The second half was true. I couldn’t fault his research, but it came a little late. My English had been excellent while it produced adjectives. It developed problems the moment it produced question marks.
“I’ve written for American and European organizations for over 15 years,” I told him. “My English has never been a problem. Until now.”

items: I'm fluent in English, but my accent still feels like a barrier to acceptance

blocks.text: I was angry. Of all the things I expected to have to prove in Canada, my English wasn’t on the list.
I ended up leaving the company. My English came with me. We had been through a lot together.
It’s been more than two years since. The bitterness has aged nicely, like cheddar.

Meanwhile, my English and I went freelance. Not one client told me my English was so good. Or so bad. They asked for a redraft when one was needed and sent more work. I recommend this as a form of compliment. It’s quieter and you can invoice for it.

These days I work for a global company with people in Canada, the U.S. and Europe. People here have opinions, too. They tell me when a piece is great and when I’ve got the technology totally wrong. Not one of them has an opinion about my English. A plumber is judged on the pipes. Nobody asks where the wrench is from. I've never been so happily criticized.
English is still not my first language. It's still doing very well. It even has Canadian experience now.
Thank you for asking.
Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

A journalist based in Saskatoon, Anusuya has a keen interest in connecting technology with sustainability and social causes, and writes for various tech media platforms. She has also delivered guest lectures at the University of British Columbia’s school of journalism on the use of satellite imagery in storytelling.

articles.title: Facing 'uncomfortable' questions, King Charles shows the 'soft power' of the Crown
articles.summary: As with trips to Canada in 2025 and the United States earlier this year, King Charles's recent visit to the Caribbean saw him walking something of a diplomatic tightrope at a politically charged…

image.caption: King Charles greets local residents holding national flags during a visit to Nelson's Dockyard, a historic naval base established in 1725, in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, on Nov. 2. (Isabel Infantes/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As King Charles was wrapping up his recent trip to the Caribbean and South America, a palace aide let it be known via news reports that he relishes the "tough parts" of his role as monarch and would keep being used in "politically charged" deployments.

There's little doubt the nine-day sojourn was one of the tougher outings of his four-year reign, shrouded as it was in questions about whether the U.K. should apologize for its role in the transatlantic slave trade and pay reparations.
During the trip that took Charles to Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, he spoke of the "great suffering and injustices of the past" and called the slave trade a "shameful chapter."
No apology emerged, but U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham indicated as the visit was unfolding that he was open to calls for a formal apology, a marked change in British policy on the issue.

Burnham rejected calls for financial reparations. But writing in the Guardian newspaper, he said he wanted to "launch a new drive on debt," which included helping more vulnerable countries "repay over a longer time period and with better ⁠rates."
As with trips to Canada in 2025 and the United States earlier this year, Charles was walking something of a diplomatic tightrope at a politically charged time. There seems to be an emerging pattern.
King Charles addresses 'shameful' history of transatlantic slave trade
"He doesn't seem to shy away from uncomfortable historical questions," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

"By acknowledging them and navigating them, he's showing that these are real questions that matter to people. They can't be ignored. But also there is that tacit acknowledgment that his interest and recognition and engaging in those conversations does not direct policies of the British government."
Charles seems to be good at creating opportunities for dialogue "when a more overt political initiative or intervention would be counterproductive," Vovk said.
"So he really is demonstrating how effective the soft power of the Crown is for Britain's foreign relations."

Those relations were front and centre in the recent trip. Along with the calls for an apology and questions over reparations, there is republican pressure to remove the monarch as head of state in some countries.

Terrence Campbell, parliamentary leader of Guyana’s opposition group A Partnership for National Unity, holds placards during a demonstration demanding a formal British apology and reparations for slavery and colonialism in Georgetown, Guyana, on Oct. 30. (Isabel Infantes/Reuters)

"It was a very difficult, a very challenging visit," Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, said in an interview.

"But he survived it, and survived it far better when you compare with the [2022] visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales to the Caribbean [that] attracted a huge amount of criticism in its aftermath, both in terms of how it was planned and how the events took place."
That trip had been seen by some as a bid to shore up ties between Britain and the Commonwealth countries on its itinerary: Belize, Jamaica and the Bahamas.

In the end, that weeklong visit drew more headlines for protests, the republican sentiment fomenting particularly in Jamaica, calls for slavery reparations and uncomfortable moments that seemed more rooted in the colonial past than looking toward the future.

items: What should a royal visit look like? Why William and Kate's recent trip might spark change for future tours

blocks.text: This time, Rowbotham said, Charles made it clear that "as far as he was concerned, it was a matter for the Caribbean communities to make a choice about who should be their head of state."
"He was happy to continue to serve but it was something which he would not fight if they made a different decision."
Charles carried out numerous engagements in the three countries he visited, with many focusing on issues he has made a priority, including the environment and conservation, youth and sustainability.

An Indigenous child, right, presents King Charles, left, with a traditional beaded necklace during a meeting with Indigenous leaders at the National Toshaos Council at Umana Yana on Oct. 30 in Georgetown, Guyana. (Ben Stansall/Getty Images)
Any royal visit has its moments. This one had the umbrella — or initial lack thereof for the King — as the skies opened up in Antigua and Barbuda.
"He was initially clearly taken aback when there was no handy umbrella," Rowbotham said.
"He subsequently laughed it off and simply carried on," she said, calling it "the mark of a monarch who knows how to be diplomatic in a stressful situation."
King Charles gets soaked in Antigua as Camilla gets only umbrella
The moment reminded Vovk of the time Charles got frustrated over a pen holder while signing documents during the ceremony confirming him as monarch in 2022.
"He has certainly gotten better at being able to laugh about those sorts of things."
Remembering the fallen
Queen Camilla, left, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, attend the Remembrance Sunday ceremony at the Cenotaph on Whitehall in central London on Nov. 8. (Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images)
Members of the Royal Family honoured the memory of the fallen at annual events around London in recent days.

King Charles led the tributes on Remembrance Sunday at a ceremony attended by thousands of veterans at the Cenotaph in central London. While Charles, Prince William and others laid wreaths, Queen Camilla, Catherine, Princess of Wales, and others watched from the balcony of a nearby building.
The night before, Charles and Camilla led senior members of the Royal Family for an evening of remembrance at Royal Albert Hall.
Princess Anne, front centre, and Prince William attend the National Service of Remembrance at the Cenotaph on Nov. 8 in London, England. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)
A few days earlier, Birgitte, the Duchess of Gloucester, on behalf of Camilla, opened the 98th Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey.
The remembrance events are a high point of the royal ceremonial year.
The events were little changed from previous years, something that stood out to Vovk.
"This is where ritual culture becomes so important for reinforcing consistency and values across generations," he said.
"It is something that unites the Crown and the people in memory, in grief, in a sense of responsibility."
Birgitte, Duchess of Gloucester, centre, looks on during her visit to the 98th Field of Remembrance at Westminster Abbey on Nov. 5 in London. (Alberto Pezzali/Getty Images)
Meghan's father cut off monitor days after arrest, officials say

Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was in custody this week after authorities in Florida said he cut off an ankle monitor days after his arrest on allegations of keeping child sexual abuse materials.

Meghan hasn't commented publicly in recent days, and pulled out of a speech she had been planning to give in Belgium on Tuesday. She appeared that day with her husband, Prince Harry, as he spoke at the European Parliament in Brussels.

Earlier, however, Meghan had said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about her father had been sent to London police in 2019.
"I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."
Meghan Markle's father arrested, charged over child sexual abuse images

Media attention for several years has focused on the estrangement, and observers see the possibility recent events could influence public perceptions around Meghan, which have been polarizing in some quarters.

"I'm sure the British public and the wider public, you know, in the States and elsewhere, will have sympathy for her in regards to what's emerged about her father," royal commentator Roya Nikkah told CBC News.
Vovk sees the current situation could "dramatically shift public perception" of Meghan and could "soften public criticism and public reactions" to her.

items: Meghan Markle's father cut off ankle monitor days after arrest, U.S. officials say
Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material

blocks.text: He also wonders if it might help clear the way for some level of rapprochement between Meghan, Harry and the Royal Family.
"I don't know if I'd say a road to reconciliation, but perhaps an opportunity for some mutual support between the Sussexes and the rest of the Royal Family."
The King and the Rocket Man
Elton John, left, and King Charles pose for a photograph at Apple Music Studios, where they were recording John's Rocket Hour, in London, in October. (Apple Music/Reuters)
It's long been known that King Charles has a love of music, particularly of the classical persuasion. But his latest public musings on the overall matter have little royal precedent.
Charles sat down at a microphone opposite Elton John to take part in a special edition of the singer's show.

The episode of Elton John's Rocket Hour aired Saturday — Charles's 78th birthday — on Apple Music. It's intended to celebrate 50 years of the King's Trust — founded by Charles with his navy severance pay as the Prince's Trust in 1976 — and musicians who have supported the youth charity.

"Music has ​always been at the heart of the Prince's, and now the King's Trust," Charles said, adding that the program offered a chance to showcase performers who had supported the charity ​and newer artists it had helped launch.

In a release, Buckingham Palace said the episode also highlights artists — such as the rock band Muse — who received help from the trust at the beginning of their careers, and in some cases went on to support it as alumni.

Muse, which started out in 1994 under the name Rocket Baby Dolls, received a grant from the Prince's Trust to buy sound equipment. In 2018, the band performed a sold-out concert at the Royal Albert Hall in support of the trust.
Charles, left, meets John as he arrives for the Royal Variety Performance at the Royal Albert Hall in London, on Nov. 22, 2024. (Toby Melville/Reuters)
Charles and John shared memories of performances by musicians in support of the charity's initiatives — from rock galas at Wembley Arena to concerts in Hyde Park.
"If ⁠you champion a young artist and show you believe in them, it makes all the difference," John said. "Young people are ​our future."
Vovk saw little precedent for Charles sitting down across the table from John.
"It's potentially groundbreaking. I think this is the first time that the sovereign has done something that would be classified in this way as entertainment," he said.

"To actually sit down and have a recorded conversation with the sovereign is extraordinarily rare. Elizabeth did a few of them in her final years, but these were all about reminiscences around the Crown jewels, coronation ceremony, her father…. To have something that is so, well, mainstream, is really unheard of."

John, second from left, Charles and Tim Cook, Apple's executive chairman, pose with mentees during a music workshop for young peopleat Battersea Power Station in southwest London, on Oct. 7. (Ben Stansall/Reuters)
Royally quotable
"I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time. This is the same in nature."
— Catherine, Princess of Wales, regarding her recovery from cancer. She made the comment in an interview in an issue of Country Life magazine that was guest-edited by her husband, Prince William.
Royal reads

Prince William has expressed his frustration at the way women are treated in the military. The future head of the British Armed Forces has been holding under-the-radar meetings with female service personnel as part of a drive to ensure they feel "safe, respected and valued." [Daily Mail]
Prince William's Duchy of Cornwall has apologized to tenants for its handling of the sale of an estate in southwestern England and promised new valuations of their farms and homes. [The Observer]
Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh, told Rohingya refugees in the camps at Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh "we won't walk away" after hearing about the hardships they face. [The Independent]

Prince Harry and five other prominent figures have launched a legal challenge against a judge's verdict in their unsuccessful claims against the Daily Mail's publisher, Associated Newspapers. [The Guardian]
The Princess of Wales met with families gaining extra support for their youngsters' social development at a community hospital in southern England. [ITV]

The Prince of Wales made another European away trip in support of soccer team Aston Villa as he attended a Champions League match against Barcelona. William was joined by his son, Prince George. [ESPN]
Prince George contributed a colourful drawing of a kingfisher to the edition of Country Life guest-edited by his father. [Country Life]
Catherine, Princess of Wales, left, meets Ruby, nine months old, during a visit to the Chase Community Hospital on Wednesday in Bordon, England. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)

articles.title: AI cheating scandal rattles South Korea as annual college exam looms
articles.summary:
Fears for national entrance exam next week, as top scorer on tax exam admits sending photos of questions to AI tool

The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for…

blocks.text: The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true. On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat.

The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

“I cheated using ⁠electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the top score was not ​the result of fair effort,” the candidate said, ‌identifying himself by the ‌surname Han, as he apologised on the YouTube channel Attorney Lee Don-ho.

Han, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.
Speaking on camera wearing a face mask, Han said he had submitted a written confession to Seoul police.

The Seoul metropolitan police agency said: “We received a written confession through the test taker’s lawyer this morning regarding cheating on the tax accountant exam,” adding that the case had been assigned to investigators.

The scandal has rattled a ‌country where standardised tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories. It comes just days before Thursday’s annual national college entrance exam, ‌a high-pressure event for which many South ​Korean students will have spent much of their lives preparing.

“The presidential office views ​the matter very seriously, and because the college entrance exam is next week, we have been working hard to prepare countermeasures,” a senior presidential office official told reporters on Sunday.

The official said that reports of potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam were concerning, adding ⁠that the presidential chief of staff for policy would convene an emergency meeting later ​in the afternoon to ​address the issue.

The prime minister, Han Seong-sook, acknowledged on Friday public concerns over AI-assisted cheating. The government would “prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably”, a statement from her office said.
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this article

articles.title: Macron urges unity as Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia
articles.summary: Leaders of French-speaking nations gathered in Phnom Penh as a row over who should lead the Francophonie and Congo’s threat to quit put pressure on Macron to broker consensus.

image.caption: Cambodia is taking over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, after France served as the host nation in 2024Image: Soveit Yarn/REUTERS

blocks.text: A summit of French-speaking nations opened Sunday in Phnom Penh, with French President Emmanuel Macron trying to head off a walkout by the group's biggest African member over who will lead it next.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) brings together about 90 states and governments, including 53 full members, from the Democratic Republic of Congo to Canada.
It is made up of countries that use French as an official language, former French colonies, and other states with substantial historic ties to France.
What is the disagreement about?
The OIF is set to choose its next secretary-general on Monday.

Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who has held the post since 2018, is seeking a third term. DR Congo has threatened to leave if she is re-elected, accusing Rwanda of backing the M23 armed group in eastern Congo, an accusation Rwanda denies.

DR Congo has 57.3 million French speakers, second only to France, per the OIF, so its exit would be a major blow. Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew from the association last year after their membership was suspended over coups.
On Saturday, DR Congo said it was withdrawing its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country's martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.
Kinshasa said it would back former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos to allow "consensus around a unifying candidacy."
AFP described the offer as conditional on Rwanda also stepping aside. However, Rwanda's foreign minister said Mushikiwabo would stay in the race.
What did Macron say?
Macron warned against "internal fractures" in the group.
"We must ensure that we preserve what constitutes its strength—namely, its unity," he said.
Rwanda said Macron had asked President Paul Kagame to withdraw his candidate, which it refused. Macron's office said Paris suggested both candidates step aside.

"With that intervention we're going backwards, to the idea that France decides," a member of a non-African delegation told AFP anonymously. France is the largest donor, and Canada provides 25% of the budget.
Macron arrives amid unrest at home, where more than 600,000 people marched earlier this month over wages and in support of student protests, with thousands arrested.

UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews urged delegates to press Cambodia, which has been referred to as a de facto one-party state, to free detained activists. "No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions," he said.

articles.title: Marcos urges ASEAN members to strengthen regional ties
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Sunday urged Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member-states to strengthen partnerships and cooperation in addressing challenges facing the region.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 4:02pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Sunday urged Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member-states to strengthen partnerships and cooperation in addressing challenges facing the region.
Marcos made the call during the plenary session of the 49th ASEAN Summit, where he outlined the Philippines' priorities as this year's chair: peace and security, prosperity, and people empowerment.
"Our institutions must become better at working across pillars and sectors, drawing on the strengths of governments, business, civil society, academia, and our people," he said.

"Our partnerships should continue to advance ASEAN priorities, respond to the needs of our member states, and turn political goodwill into practical cooperation, with ASEAN at the center of the regional architecture that we have built," he added.
During the summit's opening ceremony, Marcos said the gathering provides an opportunity for member-states to address the region's pressing challenges.
These include transnational crimes such as human trafficking, cybercrime, and online scams, as well as the need to strengthen maritime cooperation.
The 49th ASEAN Summit opened on Sunday, with delegates arriving at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance
articles.summary: Events are being held for Volkstrauertag, a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts say the country is headed for a budget crisis. DW has more.

image.caption: The Neue Wache in Berlin is the central German memorial for victims of warImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 15, 2026
Germany marks day of mourning for victims of war and oppression

blocks.caption: Germany is remembering victims of war and oppressionImage: imago images/Udo Gottschalk

blocks.text: Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.
Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.
There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.
In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.
Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.
"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

articles.title: Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles
articles.summary: Three months after leaving Lopez Inc., Gabby Lopez’s new game plan is clear

blocks.text: Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

When Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III sold his family’s shares in the main Lopez holding company in August, he said the move would allow his family to “channel our family’s resources into businesses aligned with our personal mission,” adding that more announcements would come in due time.
Three months later, his new game plan is clear. It centers on two companies that serve everyday Filipinos: ABS-CBN and Rockwell Land.

On Thursday, November 12, First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), led by Gabby’s cousin, Federico “Piki” Lopez, agreed to sell its 90.74% voting stake in Rockwell Land. The buyer is Gabby’s and his siblings’ private firm, Crème Investment Corporation, and the price tag is P15.92 billion.

This completes a 94-day asset swap that began on August 10. Back then, Crème sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. to San Miguel boss Ramon S. Ang for about P11 billion. Lopez Inc. was originally built as the untouchable top holding company meant to protect the family empire from outside takeovers. (READ: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN)

blocks.caption: THEN…The Rockwell property with  the old Meralco power plant (upper right) in Makati City. Rappler/Rockwell brand rap file image

blocks.text: For decades, Rockwell Land has been the Lopez Group’s luxury lifestyle and consumer jewel. Started in 1995 on the site of an old Meralco power plant in Makati, Rockwell turned an industrial lot into Rockwell Center, which is now home to Power Plant Mall, high-end condos, serviced apartments, and offices.

blocks.caption: …AND NOW. Bird’s eye view of Rockwell Makati with Power Plant Mall at the center. Courtesy of Rockwell Land

blocks.text: This focus on everyday consumers is a natural fit for Gabby who spent his career in TV, entertainment, and public-facing brands. Just two days after the August sale, Gabby and his cousins pledged P2.2 billion of their own money to help rebuild ABS-CBN. He explained why: “ABS-CBN has been part of this family for generations. The mission our family set out to pursue remains the heartbeat of this family—to be in the service of the Filipino. We are putting our own money behind this conviction.” (READ: Gabby Lopez: Man on a mission)

This is a sharp contrast from Piki Lopez’s world at FPH and First Gen, an ascetic, heavy-infrastructure universe of geothermal steam fields, gas turbines, and pumped-storage hydropower projects that require tens of billions of pesos and years, sometimes decades, of engineering before they make money. At the 2026 annual stockholders’ meetings of FPH and First Gen, Piki repeatedly framed his leadership around the “compounding” value of long-term choices, and that “direction over speed” matters more. In other words, a slow-and-steady approach built for power grids rather than quick profits.
Gabby does not seem to be retreating from the family business. Instead, he is separating the group’s lifestyle and media brands from FPH’s power business and bringing them under his own control.

blocks.caption: BOSS. Ambassador Manuel “Manolo” Lopez speaks at a corporate event following Rockwell Land Corp.’s listing on May 12, 2012, in Rockwell Power Plant Mall’s premises in Makati City. Courtesy of Rockwell Land FB

blocks.text: Rockwell also has deep ties to Gabby’s late uncle, Manuel “Manolo” Lopez. Manolo ran Meralco for over 30 years and was deeply disappointed when the family and business group, both led then by his older brother Oscar, the father of Piki, forced FPH to let go of Meralco in 2009 to pay off First Gen’s geothermal debts. Manolo was quoted then saying, “Meralco would have been my parents’ legacy.” In March and April 2026, Manolo’s children joined Gabby and other cousins in publicly challenging Piki’s leadership. Buying Rockwell brings a business closely linked to Manolo’s side of the family under Crème’s direct control.
Beyond family history and culture, this deal solves a major money problem for Gabby’s branch: ABS-CBN needs cash, and Rockwell makes it.

In 2025, Rockwell earned P4.73 billion. ABS-CBN lost P4.72 billion. Crème has already pledged P766.7 million to ABS-CBN’s P6-billion fundraising drive. Buying Rockwell gives Gabby’s family an established, profitable company that brings in its own money. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

blocks.caption: CASH COW. Rockwell Land’s 2025 earnings. Courtesy of Rockwell Land website

blocks.text: Before losing its broadcast franchise in 2020, ABS-CBN was a reliable cash machine for its parent firm, Lopez Holdings, former Benpres Holdings and one level below Lopez Inc in the Lopez group shareholder tree. ABS-CBN paid Lopez Holdings P447 million in dividends in 2018 and P269 million in 2019. Once the network went off the air, those payouts vanished. From 2020 to 2025, ABS-CBN racked up about P45.5 billion in losses. (READ: ABS-CBN is now 84% content — and still losing money. Can P6 billion fix it?)

With ABS-CBN out of cash, Lopez Holdings had to lean almost completely on FPH, which owns the group’s power and property businesses. From 2021 to 2025, FPH paid Lopez Holdings a flat P567 million a year in dividends. After Lopez Holdings paid its bills and shared profits with public stockholders, only about P247 million actually reached Lopez, Inc. in 2025.

FPH’s own financial records show where that money came from. In 2025, subsidiary Rockwell paid FPH roughly P630 million in dividends. Meralco—where FPH still owns a 3.95% stake—paid another P1.115 billion. Together, those two companies gave FPH P1.75 billion in cash dividends. That is more than triple the P567 million FPH sent up to Lopez Holdings.

FPH didn’t just hoard the extra cash. As a public company, it had debts, operating costs, outside shareholders, and massive power projects to pay for. First Gen and its subsidiary, Energy Development Corporation, were pouring money into geothermal drilling, hydropower, and battery storage while paying off loans. First Gen President and COO Giles Puno noted at this year’s annual meeting that while the company aims to pay out 30% of its yearly recurring profit, those payouts depend on spending needs, growth plans, and debt payments. To save cash, First Gen cut how much it paid as yearly dividend to its parent FPH from P0.90 per share in 2024 to P0.80 in 2025.

So most of the Piki-led power group’s profits stayed locked inside the operating companies. For family members at the very top of the corporate ladder, including Gabby and the heirs of Manolo, that meant waiting years for bigger payouts. Buying Rockwell lets Crème skip all those corporate middlemen. Instead of waiting for cash to trickle up through FPH, Lopez Holdings, and Lopez, Inc., Gabby’s firm can soon collect dividends straight from the source as Rockwell’s main owner.

blocks.caption: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target

blocks.text: Rockwell’s net profit for parent shareholders climbed from P3.11 billion in 2023 to P3.71 billion in 2024, reaching P4.73 billion in 2025. The 2025 number got a boost from a one-time gain after buying Alabang Commercial Corporation. Even without that extra boost, Rockwell still earned about P4.1 billion.

Its cash flow has grown right along with its profits. Rockwell brought in P2 billion in cash from daily operations in 2025, up sharply from P144 million in 2024, even though real estate requires heavy upfront spending on land and construction. Its regular dividends grew steadily too, rising from P0.0752 per share in 2023 to P0.1018 in 2024, and hitting P0.1212 in 2025. Renting out commercial spaces gives Rockwell a steady safety net beyond just selling condos. Power Plant Mall in Makati, its office buildings, and its December 2025 purchase of Alabang Commercial Corporation—which added Alabang Town Center and a nearby office tower—bring in reliable rental cash.

blocks.caption: Refreshed Alabang Town Center? What shoppers can expect now that Rockwell has near-full control.

blocks.text: Of course, Rockwell has big bills of its own. Its P21.6-billion Alabang deal is being paid in installments through December 2027, and it raised P10 billion in retail bonds in March 2026 to fund active projects. It can’t pay dividend to its owners every single peso it makes. Still, it gives Gabby a healthy business that makes money rather than drains it.
Rockwell and ABS-CBN share more than just the Lopez family name. Over the last four years, Rockwell has been one of the main buyers of the real estate ABS-CBN sold to raise cash.

In 2022, Rockwell bought properties from ABS-CBN for P786 million, followed by another P733 million deal in 2023. Those sales gave the network profit gains of P246 million and P232 million. In 2024, Rockwell bought more ABS-CBN land for about P679 million—booking a P223.1-million gain for the broadcaster—and agreed to buy ABS-CBN’s Iloilo property for P91.4 million. Later company filings showed even more property deals between the two firms.

Their shared history goes back even further. Before Rockwell went public in 2012, its housing arm built the 53 Benitez condos in Quezon City on the site of an old movie studio. Lopez Holdings, then known as Benpres Holdings, also owned 24.5% of Rockwell directly before selling it to FPH in August 2009.

Smaller day-to-day ties are still in place. ABS-CBN Holdings Corporation, which handles the network’s depository receipts, keeps its main office at Rockwell Business Center Sheridan in Mandaluyong. Lopez Holdings also pays office rent to Rockwell.

No merger or money-sharing plan between Rockwell and ABS-CBN has been announced, and they remain completely separate companies. Still, Rockwell has repeatedly stepped in to buy the properties ABS-CBN needed to sell, and now Gabby is taking over Rockwell itself.
Until August, Crème’s 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. gave Gabby’s family a small, indirect piece of several businesses, but very little control over dividend payouts.

Under the P15.92-billion deal approved by FPH on November 12, Crème will buy 86.58% of Rockwell’s common shares, plus voting preferred shares that raise its total voting power to 90.74%. Once regulators approve the deal and Crème makes a required buyout offer to the remaining public stockholders, it becomes the controlling owner. That gives Crème a direct say over Rockwell’s board and dividend payouts, within the limits of corporate law, loan rules, and minority shareholder rights.

If Rockwell keeps paying its 2025 dividend rate of P0.1212 per share, Crème’s incoming block of 5.30 billion common shares would bring in about P642 million a year before taxes. Future payouts aren’t guaranteed—they will depend on Rockwell’s profits, spending needs, and board votes.

Three months after leaving Lopez, Inc., Gabby Lopez’s new game plan is clear. He has fresh cash for ABS-CBN, the network he spent his life building, and direct control of Rockwell Land, a profitable lifestyle developer that already makes money. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
articles.summary:
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit…

blocks.text: Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. Likened to the 1945 summit at Yalta, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.
“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.
“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.
“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”
German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.
“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine, and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.
“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

Zelensky has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”, invoking the conference in Crimea when the then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.
“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.
“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.
“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo. It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.
More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

articles.title: Party-list reform bill may be tackled in 2027 ahead of 2028 polls - Adiong
articles.summary: The House of Representatives may begin plenary discussions on a proposed measure reforming the party-list system next year, the chair of the House Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms said…

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 2:01pm

The House of Representatives may begin plenary discussions on a proposed measure reforming the party-list system next year, the chair of the House Committee on Suffrage and Electoral Reforms said Sunday.
Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said Congress still has time to tackle House Bill No. 9906 before the 2028 national elections, although the pace of deliberations remains uncertain.
“Palagay ko baka ma-tackle na ito next year na,” Adiong told Super Radyo dzBB.
“I think this might be tackled next year,” he said.
“Mayroon pa tayong isang taon bago tayo magkaroon ng presidential elections. Hindi lang natin sigurado kung paano yung flow ng debate,” he added.

Among the key provisions of HB 9906 is a proposed ban on individuals within the second degree of consanguinity or affinity to incumbent senators or House members from being nominated as party-list representatives.

The measure also requires party-list organizations to certify that they were not established by political dynasties and are not linked to individuals with beneficial interests in government contracts.
Adiong said a technical working group had already been formed to study the proposed measure.
He said the committee was hoping to submit its report to the plenary before the year ends to allow deliberations to begin.
“Before the end of this year, magre-report na tayo kung makasingit pa po tayo sa plenaryo ng ating committee report, nang sa ganun magsimula na po ang debate,” he said.— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: World’s top court to rule if Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
articles.summary:
International court of justice has never before found a state guilty of genocide, and ruling will have implications for case against Israel

The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this…

blocks.text: The world’s top court will deliver a judgment this week on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, in a landmark case that will set a critical 21st-century benchmark for the gravest of all international crimes.
The closely watched judgment could become one of the most significant moments in international law since the end of the second world war.

The international court of justice (ICJ) has never found a state responsible for genocide, a crime defined after the Nazi-led Holocaust. The ruling will have implications for a separate high-profile genocide case against Israel.
Nearly a decade after a military campaign forced hundreds of thousands of Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border, the ICJ in The Hague will deliver its judgment on Thursday morning.
“The ICJ ruling will be historic for Rohingya survivors and their families around the world,” said Yanghee Lee, a former UN rights investigator to Myanmar.

“The international community failed to prevent Myanmar military atrocities against the Rohingya nine years ago. It must seize this opportunity to finally secure justice for the Rohingya and begin to reckon with these failings.”

blocks.caption: The Kutupalong Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Munir Uz Zaman/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: ICJ judges have spent seven years weighing accusations by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, that Myanmar’s repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN genocide convention.
A key issue in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Antonia Mulvey, the founder of Legal Action Worldwide (Law), a group that represents hundreds of Rohingya survivors, said she was “cautiously optimistic” the court would hold Myanmar fully accountable.
Government actions showed “patterns of conduct” that proved clear attempts to destroy the group, she said.

“The attacks on the villages took place the same way,” she said. “They would attack the civilians, burn the villages, separate men and women, conduct sexual violence … and then as they fled, they would continue to kill them.”

Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the Balkans fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent the genocide at Srebrenica.

Mulvey said a key part of the upcoming judgment will be how it handles the issue of rape and sexual violence as an act of genocide. Her team has collected accounts of soldiers mutilating women’s genitals and biting their faces. “That’s to mark people, to brand them … it is also to stop reproduction,” she said.
“Yes, we would say sexual violence is a critical part to show their intent to destroy the group,” she added.

“You don’t need to gang-rape people. You don’t need to kill their children in front of them. You don’t need to mutilate them. You don’t need to do it in public. What is the purpose of that? The purpose is to destroy the group.”

In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear directly from Rohingya survivors who travelled from camps in Bangladesh. One witness said her child was taken from her arms, stabbed and thrown into a fire, according to Law, while another described seeing piles of bodies in a mass grave.
During hearings, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”.
“It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents.

For decades, Rohingya people have been stripped of their citizenship and targeted by increasing discrimination, amid a backdrop of communal violence with Buddhists in the country’s western Rakhine state.
The crisis reached a climax after a Rohingya militant group conducted guerrilla-style attacks in the summer of 2017. The Myanmar army responded with massive “clearance operations”.

Refugees who fled into Bangladesh in 2017 told the Guardian of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, including the drowning of children in a river.
This testimony from Tula Toli – which satellite footage later showed had been razed – added to dozens of witness accounts collected over the years to build a case for genocide.

A ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would add international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-2017 attacks and later overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a military airstrike on a market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, a rebel-held area in western Rakhine state, 28 September 2026. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images
