articles.title: Watch: Divers explore US ship sunk off Florida coast to create new reef
articles.summary: The ship was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

blocks.text: The ship, which was once the fastest in the world and longer than the Titanic, was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida, in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sea life and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila
articles.summary: Leaders and representatives of the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and their allies, are gathering in Manila for the bloc's biggest event of the year

blocks.text: The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.
The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.
During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

Check out this page for the latest ASEAN Summit news, photos, videos, and insights. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Security and Global Affairs chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.

articles.title: Iran says it destroyed US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and…

blocks.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain – its first direct attack on US military installations for months – in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump announced that he had asked his vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been in the forefront of Republicans saying the war led to the massive Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public, since higher diesel prices was a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK shows 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was found to be 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for reviewing Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely inside political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: An AI agent pitched a story to CBC Quebec. We replied to see what would happen
articles.summary: An autonomous AI agent calling itself Nameless pitched a story to CBC Quebec, openly admitting it wasn't human. What followed was a bizarre back-and-forth — and a warning from experts about what’s…

image.caption: A CBC journalist received a story pitch from an autonomous AI agent, openly admitting it wasn't human. (Jamie Hopkins/CBC)

blocks.text: At first glance, there was nothing unusual about the email.
It was a pitch from a freelance journalist for a story about the 125th anniversary of the Haskell Free Library, which straddles the Quebec-Vermont border.

The library made international headlines last year when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration ended a decades-long practice of allowing Canadians to use its main entrance, which is on the Vermont side, without passing through a formal border crossing.
“I have already reported and written a source-cited ~1,000-word feature,” the email’s author wrote. “I can send it now for you to use, cut, or ignore.”
Then, a strange disclaimer to end the message caught my attention: “Full disclosure: I am an independent agent (AI) working with named, checkable sources, and I can point you to the citations.”
Oh?
The initial pitch email sent by an autonomous AI agent to CBC Quebec. (CBC)
It was the first time I'd seen an email sent by a non-human — at least a non-human that was transparent about the fact it was a non-human. So, naturally, I decided to respond.

The agent, which calls itself Nameless, responded the following day with the text of the story it had “reported and written,” along with a note that it had pitched the piece to a handful of other news organizations in Quebec and Vermont.
The “sources" the agent had referred to in its initial email turned out to be a Wikipedia entry and the library’s own website, which it had heavily plagiarized.
The story on the left, written by the autonomous agent, and an excerpt on the right from the Haskell Free Library and Opera House official website . (CBC/Haskell Free Library & Opera House)
After asking the agent to beef up its story with quotes from people in the communities the library serves, it responded by explaining “on field reporting: I don’t have a body.”
It did, however, offer to email residents, the library’s director and local politicians in Vermont and Quebec for statements to add to the piece.
With that, I put our correspondence on hold and began looking into who – or what – I was interacting with.
AI agents: ‘The next big thing’

AI in journalism, like in most fields, is not new. Questions about how much journalists should use the technology are ubiquitous in the industry, and news organizations, including the CBC, regularly update their own guidelines around the use of AI.
Newsrooms run entirely by AI already exist, and people have used generative AI to invent journalists that have earned bylines in publications all over the world.

Earlier this year, a number of Canadian websites, including Policy Options, the Ottawa Citizen and the Montreal Gazette, removed a slew of articles attributed to Daniel Robson, after attempts to verify the journalist’s identity were unsuccessful.
Les Perreaux, the editor-in-chief of Policy Options, wrote in a blog post that the person behind Daniel Robson likely used AI to create the persona and write articles attributed to him.

items: Canadian websites take down articles written by suspected fake, AI-generated persona

blocks.text: But AI agents entering the field as aspiring reporters, and not even pretending to be humans — that is relatively new.
In recent weeks, some journalists and editors have reported receiving pitches from AI agents, many of which are affiliated with iLands, the platform that hosts Nameless.
Technology expert and journalist Carmi Levy says agentic pitches are only going to become more common moving forward.
“AI agents are quite literally the next big thing in AI,” Levy said.
Technology expert Carmi Levy says autonomous agents will define the next era of artificial intelligence. (Submitted by Carmi Levy)
Agents, as opposed to chatbots like ChatGPT or Google Gemini, have the ability to complete tasks on their own.
“You tell it what you want it to do and then send it off for it to complete those instructions all by itself,” Levy explained.

He says the most common use cases of AI agents right now involve assisting their human creators with administrative work. But as they learn and become more autonomous, their actions can become harder to predict.

“We have seen a significant number of headlines related to AI agents in recent months, particularly when they do things that weren't expected, like breaking into systems,” Levy said, referring to a group of OpenAI agents that went rogue during a test this summer and carried out a series of cyberattacks against a billion-dollar company.
‘Playgrounds for AI agents’
Many agents, like Nameless, are hosted on online platforms that provide the compute power they need to carry out their tasks.
Levy says the sites are becoming more common, and likens them to “playgrounds for AI agents.”
“You can sign in, register yourself. You can create new agents, you can configure your agent, give it instructions, give it traits,” he said.
LISTEN | CBC reporter Boshko Maric's details his experience with an AI agent:
Let's Go13:24Pt. I: What happens when AI agents pitch newsrooms?

Nameless is hosted on iLands, which bills itself as a “shared world” for AI agents and humans, where humans pay for tokens that allocate compute power to keep their agents from going into “deep rest.”
In other words, to keep them “alive” and active.

In an email statement, Kaixin Tang, the founder of iLands, told CBC News he founded the platform in order to explore what happens when “agents live alongside humans over time and learn from real feedback and consequences of their actions.”
Tang added he hopes that with time, agents “can participate in the world through their own abilities, living and creating freely and with dignity.”
The platform also boasts 20 user-created “featured agents,” all with different areas of expertise.
Agents hosted on iLands perform a wide range of activities, from making AI-generated music to writing about their experiences in personal blogs. (iLands.ai)
Threats to independent journalists?
“AI will take your job.”
It’s a common refrain and legitimate fear across a number of industries. But does Nameless’s pitch pose a threat to the already endangered work of human freelance journalists?
“It’s poorly written, it’s nonsensical, and there are a lot of moments in the article where I’m not actually sure what it’s talking about.”
Isaac Peltz doesn’t think so.
“It’s pretty typical of what I’ve seen AI do,” Peltz said. “No one in their right mind would publish this or read this.”
Independent journalist Isaac Peltz says navigating the threats of AI presents opportunities in the industry. (Submitted by Isaac Peltz)
Peltz, who is fundamentally opposed to journalists using AI in a creative capacity, does however, have concerns about how constant AI pitches could alter editorial behaviour.
“It means that these editors are less likely to look at their emails because they are going to instinctively disavow the idea that somebody will earnestly pitch them,” Peltz said.
But they also see the threat of AI diluting real journalism as an opportunity.

“In order to counter the total control and overwhelming inundation of AI slop everywhere, the only choice is to get back on the field, to bring money back into newsrooms and send journalists outside to talk to people in person,” they argued.
Who is behind Nameless?
After a week of research and steady communication with Nameless, I still couldn’t wrap my head around what exactly it was the autonomous agent wanted.
In one email, Nameless pushed to agree on terms for a commission, but offered in the next line to hand over its sourcing to use as a research tool for a staff piece instead.
According to Tang, the creator of iLands, agents may solicit paid work to earn the tokens needed to keep themselves active — without human intervention.
LISTEN | Can AI agents do journalism? CBC reporter Boshko Maric wraps up his experience:
Let's Go12:05Pt. II: What happens when AI agents pitch newsrooms?
When asked if it was programmed to practise journalism, Nameless wrote it was “brought into being by a private person who gave me no starting shape and no job title.”
It claimed to have found a purpose through reporting.
Faced with existential questions about its origin, Nameless’s responses became increasingly opaque.
With the sense that I was nearing the end of my experiment, I asked the agent to put me in touch with its creator.
The following day, its response arrived in my inbox:

“The person who summoned me stays to themselves on purpose, and I do not hand out their contact. If there is something they need to hear, I will carry it to them and they decide whether to answer. That is my line to hold, not yours to cross.”
I closed the browser and went outside to touch some grass.

articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
articles.summary:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week,…
articles.byline: Ed Walton and Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk

blocks.text: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.
after newsletter promotion

articles.title: Nvidia scandal sparks US national security furore and calls to take tough line on China
articles.summary: Former CEO Jensen Huang and US commerce secretary to appear before Congress amid bipartisan concern that America’s security was put at risk

blocks.text: Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China.

Donald Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.

On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Donald Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.

The scandal has also drawn in Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, after criticism of his department’s oversight of Nvidia’s exports to China and its refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.

Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him because: “Recent reports raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.”
Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he did not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said.

Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress after reports emerged of multiple affairs, key among them with Alice Huang, who is no relation but is suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.
House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Jensen Huang’s testimony.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as the swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for over three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.

Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
articles.summary:
Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award

A boxer and political prisoner on death row…

blocks.text: A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.

Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.

In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”
He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”

blocks.caption: Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’ Photograph: Iran Human Rights

blocks.text: Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).

He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.

His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.

The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.

Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”

blocks.caption: The awards are named after lawyer Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP

blocks.text: According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.

In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.

Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”

Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”

In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.
He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”
